The shape of a job

Most jobs run through the same nine stages whatever the event is. Each one has a checklist in the library — this is the map, and the checklists are the detail. Tap a stage to open its list.

  1. 1AdvanceRead the brief, kit list, schedule, input list and stage plan. Write down the one question nobody has answered.19.9 Advancing checklist
  2. 2Warehouse prepPull, test and label. Anything unfamiliar gets identified and read about here, not on site.19.2 Warehouse prep checklist
  3. 3Load-outCount it onto the truck against the list. What is missing here is missing on site.19.3 Load-out checklist
  4. 4Load-in & buildPower, cable routes, comms and patch — agreed with the people who own them before anything is run.19.4 Load-in & build checklist
  5. 5Line checkProve one input at a time, in order, against the input list. No assumptions.19.5 Line check sheet
  6. 6Before doorsThe last calm check: levels, mutes, spares, batteries, comms, walkways clear.19.6 Show-day checklist
  7. 7ShowWatch, listen, stay ahead. Faults go through the script, not through guessing.Part 16 · Make it sound good
  8. 8Derig & returnFinish accurately even when tired. Faulty kit is labelled and quarantined, never quietly returned to stock.19.7 Derig & return checklist
  9. 9AfterThree minutes of learning log turns one shift into something you can build on.End-of-shift log guide

On a job

Use the smallest safe next action. Never guess with power, flying, safety-critical equipment or a system you have not been authorised to alter. Open Job workspace →

Before the build

  1. Find the audio lead and confirm your task.
  2. Read the latest documents, not an old screenshot.
  3. Walk cable routes and power with the people who own them.
  4. Set up one clean work area; keep cases and walkways clear.

Open build checklist

When something is wrong

  1. Make it safe; mute or stop if needed.
  2. Ask: one thing or everything? What changed?
  3. Check the cheap, obvious points first.
  4. Trace one direction through the signal path.
  5. Escalate early with a clear update.

    People
    Being easy to work with is a technical skill. These cards explain who owns what, how to help, and when to stop and ask.
    
    
    
      
    Audio lead / A1
    They need
    Accurate prep, concise updates, no unapproved changes.
    You need
    Priorities, a patch plan and permission before altering the system.
    Say
    “I’ve checked X and Y. The fault is now between A and B. Do you want me to swap the cable?”
    
      
    Warehouse & prep
    They need
    Returned kit counted, labelled and quarantined when faulty—not hidden back in stock.
    You need
    The current pull list, substitutions and the company’s labelling system.
    Say
    “This is intermittent under movement; I’ve labelled it and left it out of service.”
    
      
    Production / venue
    They need
    Early, factual risks—not last-minute panic or jargon.
    You need
    Schedule, access, client changes, house rules and decision makers.
    Say
    “This needs a decision before doors: we can do A now, or B with more time.”
    
      
    Lighting, video & staging
    They need
    Clear shared routes, respect for truss/power boundaries and no surprise repatching.
    You need
    Agreement before sharing space, power, network or comms.
    Say
    “Before I run this, is this route clear for your cable and access?”
    
      
    Artists, presenters & stage management
    They need
    Calm, practical help and no technical monologue when they are under pressure.
    You need
    Changes, requirements and a route through the right person.
    Say
    “I’m going to check that with the audio lead and come straight back to you.”
    
      
    Rigging, power & safety leads
    They need
    You to respect exclusion zones, stop instructions and authorisation limits.
    You need
    Safe access, approved positions and clear ownership.
    Say
    “I’m not authorised to change that. Who owns this system?”
    
    
    
  
    
  
    
    
    Quick guides for the job itself
    Open these when the job is familiar enough to need a prompt, not a textbook.
    
    
    The d&b rack — the short version
    1. Get the plan: box, amp, channel, output mode, setup.
    2. Test every speaker cable at prep; 4-core wherever the plan uses Mix TOP/SUB or 2-Way Active.
    3. Amps close to the boxes they drive; powerCON locked.
    4. Speaker cables into the socket the mode feeds, twisted until they click, labelled both ends.
    5. Power up last, channels muted.
    6. Check the setup on every channel against the box it's actually driving.
    7. R1 online, every amp showing; System check if you have it.
    8. Prove it one box at a time at low level, then hand over to the system tech.
    The full twelve steps are in §6.18, output modes and pins in §6.17, and if anything misbehaves, talk it through.
    
    
    End-of-shift learning log — three minutes
    1. Write the job type and your role, with no confidential client detail.
    2. Record one item you handled and what it does.
    3. Record one issue: symptom, what changed, checks made, who resolved it.
    4. Write one question to ask the right person on the next shift.
    5. Choose one five-to-ten-minute topic in this handbook before the next job.
    
    
    
    How to learn an unfamiliar piece of kit at work
    1. Ask whether you may explore it and when—not during a pressured build.
    2. Find the exact model and open its official manual.
    3. Identify inputs, outputs, power, network/control and normal status lights.
    4. Follow one safe, reversible task with an experienced person nearby.
    5. Write a small “what this box does here” note; never save over a live show file.
    
    
    How to ask for the equipment-system information
    Ask the person who owns warehouse systems rather than exporting data yourself:
    1. “I’m building a private learning app for my audio development. May I have a read-only list or screenshots of the labels and categories I am allowed to use?”
    2. Ask specifically for the fields TreebySound needs: stock name, manufacturer/model, internal label/barcode, category, case or shelf location, connector/cable type, prep notes, service status and hire-in flag.
    3. Confirm what must not be copied: client data, supplier prices, serial numbers, access credentials, job contacts or live availability.
    4. Start with one small category—microphones, DIs or common cable types—and compare the export against physical labels with a supervisor.
    5. Only then decide whether to import a cleaned reference list or simply link out to the company system. Keeping one source of truth is more important than copying everything.

    Make it safe first
    
    
    Before diagnosing anything: stop the harm. Nothing on a show is worth an injury, and nobody has ever been criticised for muting something.
    
    
    
      
    The order, every time
    
      
      
        
    1. Stop or mute. Kill the output, stop the movement, clear the area. A silent show for thirty seconds is a recoverable problem.
      2. 
        
    2. Make it safe. Isolate power at the source if it is electrical. Do not re-energise anything you did not isolate yourself.
      3. 
        
    3. Get the right person. Say what happened, where, and whether anyone is hurt — before you say anything technical.
      4. 
        
    4. Do not tidy it away. Leave the scene as it is if anyone is hurt or nearly was. It has to be reported accurately.
      5. 
        
    5. Write it down while it is fresh: time, what changed, what you saw, who you told.
      6.

    Something's wrong
    
    
    A script beats a hunch. Work the sixty seconds first, then go to the subsystem that matches what you found.
    
    
    
      
    The first sixty seconds
    Say these out loud, in order
    1. Is it safe? Mute or stop if not.
    2. One thing, or everything? That halves the search immediately.
    3. What changed? Nothing fails for no reason.
    4. Check the cheap, obvious points first — cable, connector, phantom, mute, gain, patch.
    5. Trace one direction through the signal path, and only change one thing at a time.
    6. Escalate early, with a clear update.
    Full script — 12.8
    
      
    While you work
    The rules that stop you making it worse
    1. One change at a time, and put it back if it did not help.
    2. Substitute, do not rewire — swap a known-good cable in rather than re-terminating live.
    3. Never alter a system you are not authorised to alter. Ask.
    4. Label anything you take out of service instead of returning it to stock.
    5. Log it — intermittent faults are only ever solved by notes.
    The method — 12.1
    
    
    
    
    Go to the subsystem
    
    
    
      d&b & speakONModes, NL4 pins, amp lights
      Mics & cablesNo signal, crackle, intermittent
      DI & instrumentsHum, level, ground lift
      Wireless & RFDropouts, hits, range
      ConsolesRouting, mutes, show files
      Speakers & ampsSilence, distortion, protect
      Dante & networksClocking, subscriptions, glitching
      PowerTrips, phases, what is yours
      DMX & lighting-adjacentThe faults you get blamed for
      Hum & buzzGround loops, the practical fix
      IntermittentThe ones that hide when you look
      Common patternsSymptom → likely cause
      Fault kitWhat to carry and why

    Calculators
    
    
    Six working tools for the questions that come up on site. They are sanity checks, not design software — each one says what it does not tell you.
    

    
    

    

    Level converter
    

    Move between the three ways the same voltage gets written down. Mic, line and speaker level are explained in 2.2.
    

    

    

    


    

    

    0 dBu = 0.775 V = −2.2 dBV
    

    Voltages are RMS. 0 dBu is 0.775 V, 0 dBV is 1 V — which is why the same signal reads differently on two meters.
    

    

    

    Distance & delay time
    

    How long sound takes to cover a distance — for delay stacks, time-aligning a fill, or knowing why the back of the room is late. Air temperature genuinely changes the answer over a long throw.
    

    

    

    


    

    

    

    —
    

    Does not include any delay the system itself adds — converters, networks and processing all cost time. Always confirm a delay setting by ear and with the person who owns the system.
    

    

    

    SPL over distance
    

    The inverse-square rule: in free air, every doubling of distance costs about 6 dB. Useful for sanity-checking coverage, delay-fill level and how loud the front row is compared with the mix position.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    —
    

    Free-field only. Indoors, a reflective room falls off far less than this; a line array is designed not to. Treat it as the worst case, not a measurement — and never as a substitute for a real meter when noise limits apply.
    

    

    

    Decibels & ratios
    

    Translate between a change in dB and what it actually does to the signal — and to how loud it sounds. The two ratios differ because voltage and power are not the same quantity.
    

    

    

    


    

    

    —
    

    The rules of thumb worth carrying: +6 dB doubles voltage, +3 dB doubles power, and about +10 dB is what most people call "twice as loud". Perceived loudness depends on the material and the room, so the last one is a guide, not physics.
    

    

    

    RF wavelength & antenna spacing
    

    From a frequency, the wavelength and the antenna lengths and spacings that follow from it. Answers the two questions that come up on every wireless build: how far apart do these need to be, and is that whip the right one?
    

    

    

    

    —
    

    Spacing is a starting point, not a guarantee — antenna type, height, sightline, cable loss and everything metal in the room matter more than the numbers. Always scan and coordinate properly; see Part 5 and the RF day checklist.
    

    

    

    Speaker cable loss estimator
    

    A rough, practical check for "is this cable thin enough over this distance to actually matter" — not a design tool, just enough to sanity-check a long run before you commit to it.
    

    

    

    


    

    


    

    

    —
    

    Copper, round-trip resistance, nominal load. Real speakers are not a fixed impedance, so treat this as "does this matter at all", not as a specification.
    

    
    
    
    
    The numbers behind these are explained where they belong in the library: levels in 2.2, speaker cable in 3.3, and the field figures in the pocket reference.

    What to say
    
    
    Half of support is wording. These are the sentences that get you help quickly and keep you credible.
    
    
    
      
    Reporting a fault
    Symptom, change, checks, ask
    "Channel 12 has no signal at the desk. It worked at line check. I've swapped the cable and tried a different input — the fault follows the mic. Do you want me to swap the mic, or leave it and flag it?"
    Four parts, in that order: what is wrong, what changed, what you have already eliminated, and the specific permission you are asking for.
    
      
    Stopping safely
    Refusing without a row
    "I'm not authorised to change that. Who owns this system?"
    "I need to stop this until someone qualified looks at it. Where can I find them?"
    Neither sentence is an argument, and neither needs you to know the answer — only who does.
    
      
    Under time pressure
    Offer a decision, not a problem
    "This needs a decision before doors: we can do A now, or B if we get another twenty minutes."
    Production can act on that. "It's not working" gives them nothing to act on.
    
      
    To an artist or presenter
    Calm, short, and then go
    "I'm going to check that with the audio lead and come straight back to you."
    No technical monologue when someone is about to walk on. Fix it, then explain if they ask.
    
    
    
    
    Who owns what, and what each of them needs from you, is in People in the Job Hub.
    
    
    
      
    How to ask for help without freezing
    1. Make the situation safe: mute, stop or keep clear where appropriate.
    2. State the symptom in one line: “Channel 12 has no signal at the desk.”
    3. State what changed and what you checked.
    4. Ask for the next authorised action, not a vague rescue.
    5. Watch the fix and note the reason, not only the button pressed.
    
    
    
  
    

    


    
  
    
    
    Learning pathway
    
    
    What to read, in what order, and what to do with it
    
    
    The library is 21 parts and several hundred sections. This is the route through it — five stages, each one telling you exactly which sections to read in order, what to practise on a real job before moving on, and which free training is worth doing at that point and not before.
    
    
    
      The five stagesTechnician skillsHow to learn itFree trainingYour own paceCareerOutside work
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    How the pathway works
    
    
    
      
    Order matters
    Each stage assumes the one before
    Nothing here is arbitrary. The reading in stage three only makes sense once the signal path in stage two is automatic. Skipping ahead is how people end up with certificates and no hands.
    
      
    Real work is the syllabus
    Reading unlocks doing, not the other way round
    Every stage has one practical thing to have done before you move on. If the jobs are not coming up yet, read anyway — but count the stage as open until you have done it for real.
    
      
    No clock
    Stages, not months
    Jobs come up now and then rather than every week. A stage takes as long as it takes; the ticks below are the only progress measure that means anything.
    
    
    
    
    Every tick on this page is saved on this device only. Tick a line when you have actually read it — the point is to know where you got to, not to complete a list.

    Read top to bottom. Each list is in the order to read it in, and every line opens the section itself.

    Training dates, prices and availability change — check each provider before booking. This ladder is a guide to what to practise, not a qualification; your employer decides what you're authorised to do.
    
  
    
  
    
    
    Learn it in layers
    Learn the job in layers: safe hands first, then signal flow, then systems and operating. A focused session whenever you've got twenty minutes is enough — there's no clock running.
    
    
    
      
    Stage 1
    Safe, dependable foundations
    Cables, connectors, cases, labels, manual handling, signal flow and asking before acting.
    Signal basics · Cables · Safety
    
      
    Stage 2
    Assistant to capable tech
    Builds, patching, line checks, microphones, desks and simple faults under supervision.
    Mics · Consoles · Line check
    
      
    Stage 3
    Choose depth carefully
    RF, Dante, monitors, corporate AV, recording, systems or live music—follow real work opportunities rather than collecting random courses.
    RF · Networking · Monitors
    
    
    
    
    The learning loop
    Use real work as the syllabus
    1. Early on: make the physical layer automatic—common stock, cable care, labels and safe lifting.
    2. Once that's solid: trace signal paths and support a line check; log fault patterns as you meet them.
    3. When you're ready: ask for one supervised desk, patch or wireless task; explain the result back in plain language.
    One job, one learning loop
    Turn experience into progress
    1. Before: choose one thing to notice or practise.
    2. During: ask one well-timed question and write down the answer.
    3. After: add one useful line to the learning log.
    4. Next time: use that note on a real task before studying something new.
    Open learning log guide

    Outside work: keep the conservation career alive
    You didn’t leave conservation behind — you’ve got the degree, the advanced study and real field-survey experience, tropical work included. This section isn’t “a nice hobby”; it’s about keeping that portfolio active and current while audio pays the bills, and leaning on one genuine overlap — bioacoustics — so the two careers feed each other instead of competing.
    
    
    
      
    Where your two careers meet
    Bioacoustics & passive acoustic monitoring
    The fastest-growing survey method in ecology is leaving recorders in a habitat and letting software identify what’s calling. Everything you’re now learning about mics, gain, clean recording and disciplined metadata transfers straight into it — you’d arrive already fluent in the audio half most ecologists have to learn from scratch.
    Tools & how to start →
    
      
    Make your records count
    Feed the national datasets
    Log verifiable records through iRecord or iNaturalist so they flow into the NBN Atlas and the Biological Records Centre — research-grade data used in real assessments, not a private list. At your level, think about verifying records for a scheme, or becoming a county recorder for a group you know well.
    iRecord → · NBN Atlas →
    
      
    Structured survey effort
    Keep field skills sharp on real schemes
    Standardised surveys keep your methodology current and read far better on a CV than casual sightings: BTO’s Breeding Bird Survey and WeBS, the National Bat Monitoring Programme, and local Wildlife Trust reserve surveys. Pick one tied to a site you can actually reach on a rota.
    BTO surveys → · Bat monitoring →
    
    
    
    
    
      
    Turn recording into portfolio evidence
    Run a small acoustic study of your own
    1. Deploy a low-cost recorder — an AudioMoth, or a decent handheld — at a fixed point on a repeatable schedule.
    2. Analyse with BirdNET / Raven Pro for birds, or Kaleidoscope / AnalookW for bats, keeping full metadata: date, location, habitat, weather, kit and settings.
    3. Write it up as a short methods-and-results piece. Even one season at one site is a genuine, presentable artefact.
    4. Push the verified detections back into a records scheme so the effort becomes data, not just a folder of files.
    
      
    Use the tropical experience
    Stay connected to field science remotely
    Jungle survey experience is rare and worth keeping visible. Zooniverse hosts real research projects you can contribute to from home — classifying camera-trap images and acoustic recordings, tropical work included — and platforms like Arbimon / Rainforest Connection analyse tropical soundscapes at scale. Expedition-science outfits such as Operation Wallacea also take experienced field surveyors as staff, not just students.
    Zooniverse → · More routes →
    
    
    
    
    
      
    Keep the qualification progressing
    Professional body
    Join CIEEM at graduate/associate grade and work towards Chartered Ecologist (CEcol) — it stops a degree going stale and signals you’re still active in the field.
    Keep the analytical skills warm
    QGIS and R are what ecological employers expect; your own small acoustic dataset is the perfect excuse to keep them in use.
    Stay in the literature
    British Ecological Society membership and British Wildlife magazine keep you current for very little money.
    
      
    A realistic rhythm
    Small, consistent, evidenced
    1. One structured survey visit or recorder deployment whenever the calendar allows it.
    2. One analysis or verification session — process recordings, confirm IDs, submit records.
    3. Log it. A running note of effort, method and findings becomes your portfolio with no extra work.
    Conservation & bioacoustics resources
    
    
    
    
    Genuine crossover, not a side hobby: mic technique, recording discipline, reliable metadata, RF and battery management in the field, and reading a spectrogram are all things the audio job builds daily and acoustic monitoring needs directly. Respect welfare, land access, licensing (some bat and protected-bird work is licensable) and data-sharing permissions first — you already know this, but it’s worth stating plainly for any protected-species or overseas work.

    PART 0
    How to use this thing
    Two minutes here saves you a lot of scrolling later.
    

    


    0.1 The four markers
    

    Live audio has a lot of "well, it depends". So instead of pretending there's one answer, everything in here is tagged:
    

    Standard
    The way it's normally done, and what you should default to when nobody's told you otherwise. If you do this on a job, nobody will blink.
    

    Also seen
    A different method that's common enough that you will meet someone doing it. Not wrong — often just a different house style, a different era, or a different type of gig. Know it so you don't think they've made a mistake.
    

    Watch it
    The thing that breaks kit, ruins a show, or hurts someone. These are the ones worth actually memorising.
    

    Go deeper
    Where to go and learn this properly, because it's a whole subject on its own and one paragraph won't cut it. Every one of these has a matching entry in Part 18.
    

    


    0.2 Navigating
    

    The app is five places, and everything lives in one of them. The navigation bar — along the top on a computer, along the bottom on a phone — holds all five.
    

    

    ScreenWhat it is forGo there when

    Nothing is buried: every screen carries links straight into the library, and the library links back out. You do not have to remember which screen something is on — search reaches all of it.
    

    Finding things
    

    There's no one correct way to find something in here — if one route doesn't work, another will.
    

      

    • Search — press / anywhere (or tap Library in the navigation bar) to open the search box; it filters the contents list live as you type, and Esc clears it. This searches every part of the book and every one of the five screens at once — including the ones you're not currently looking at — so use it rather than your browser's own Ctrl/⌘+F, which only sees what's on screen.
      •

      • 

    • Section numbers — every heading has one. They're stable, so notes to yourself like "look at 12.3 before Friday" will still work in a year.
      • 

    • Support — the fastest route in when you're mid-job and know roughly what kind of thing you need rather than where it lives: making it safe, fault-finding — including a fault finder you can talk to, which also walks you through setups and looks things up — the calculators, the pocket reference and the glossary are all one tap away there. On a computer the On a job now button, bottom-right, opens the same shortcuts as a menu without leaving the page you're reading.
      •

      • 

    • How-to guides — every start-to-finish, step-by-step procedure in the book, grouped by area at §19.12 and as one flat alphabetical list at §19.16.
      •

      •

      •
