      • 

    • Works with no signal — this whole book is one self-contained file with nothing pulled in from the internet, so once it's saved to your phone, laptop or a USB stick it works exactly the same in a basement venue with no signal as it does at home. Keep a copy on your phone specifically — that's the one device you'll always have with you. To pin it like an app: open the file in your phone's browser, then Share → Add to Home Screen (iPhone/Safari) or the ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen (Android/Chrome).
      • 

    • Back up your notes — the private notes, ticked checklists, progress and job workspace you build up are saved only in this browser. Now and then, open Appearance and use Export backup to save them to a file; Restore backup reads one back on a new phone or after clearing your browser. Nothing is ever sent anywhere.
      • 

    

    


    0.3 What this book assumes
    

    It assumes UK working practice, because that's where the regs and the radio frequencies come from. It assumes you're working for a hire company or in-house AV team doing a mix of corporate, live music, theatre and events — the broad "technical event" world rather than one narrow specialism. And it assumes you'd rather understand why than memorise a sequence, because the sequence changes every time and the why doesn't.
    

    Where a section is thin because the answer depends entirely on your specific kit, it says so and points you at the manual. That's not a cop-out — reading the actual manual for the actual box is the single highest-value habit in this job and almost nobody does it.
    

    


    0.4 Where you're actually starting from
    

    Six months of logging kit in and out, testing it, seeing what everything is, and being shown a setup once or twice for fun rather than for real. That's a specific and genuinely useful starting point, and it's worth being honest about what it does and doesn't give you, because this book is written to build from exactly here.
    

    What it gives you: you already know what the kit is — what a stagebox looks like, roughly what lives in which flightcase, what a DI box does even if you've never wired one into a show yourself. That's the vocabulary most beginners spend their first month just acquiring. You skipped that month.
    

    What it doesn't give you yet: the muscle memory of doing it under a bit of pressure, with someone waiting, without someone more experienced quietly fixing your mistakes before you notice them. That only comes from reps — and you haven't had many yet. That's completely normal at six months, whatever it might feel like watching someone who's done it for years make it look easy.
    

    Standard
    Read this book in the order it's written the first time through, even the bits that feel basic — the basics are exactly where "I sort of know this" quietly turns into a real gap under pressure. After that, use it as a reference: search for what you need, when you need it.
    

    Go deeper
    If "in the order it's written" is too blunt an instruction, the learning pathway breaks it into five stages and tells you exactly which sections to read at each one, what to practise on a real job before moving on, and which free training is worth doing at that point rather than later.
    

    Two parts are worth flagging specifically for where you are right now. Part 12 (Fault-finding) is written to be usable even before you have deep intuition for this stuff — it gives you an actual procedure to follow, not just "get a feel for it", because a script beats a feeling every time when someone's looking at you expectantly. And §9.8 onwards covers Avolites Titan in real depth, because you've already got a head start there that's worth building on properly rather than leaving half-used.
    

    Also seen
    Nobody who's good at this job was born knowing it. Every engineer whose fault-finding looks like a magic trick got there by fixing the same handful of problems dozens of times each until the pattern-matching became automatic. You're not behind — you're at the very start of building exactly that.
    

    


    


    

    PART 1
    How a job runs & who owns what
    The working day, the people around you, paperwork and the habits that make you dependable.
    

    


    1.1 What the role actually is
    

    "Audio technician" in the event world is really four jobs wearing one coat, and which one you're doing changes by the day:
    

    

    Warehouse
    Prep, test, pack, unpack, fault-find, maintain, keep the stock honest. You're doing this bit already. It's the foundation — a well-prepped job barely goes wrong on site.
    

    Crew
    Load in, push boxes, run cable, build stacks, take direction. Physical, fast, and where you learn the most by watching.
    

    Tech
    Actually setting things up and making them work — patching, powering, testing, line-checking, fixing. This is the step you're moving into.
    

    Operator
    Mixing the show, or running playback, or looking after monitors. The visible job, and the one everyone thinks is the whole job. It isn't.
    

    

    Most people move roughly along that line, but not cleanly — you'll be crewing on Monday, teching on Wednesday, and back in the warehouse Friday. That's normal and it's a good thing. The best techs are the ones who've done every part of the chain, because when something breaks on site they know what happened to it in the van.
    

    


    1.2 The lifecycle of a hire
    

    Everything you touch is somewhere on this loop. Knowing where you are on it tells you what your job is right now.
    

      

    1. Enquiry & spec — client asks for something, someone works out what kit answers it. Produces a kit list.
      2. 

    2. Prep — kit pulled from shelves, tested, assembled into racks and cases, consumables added. Produces a packed job.
      3. 

    3. Load out — onto the van/truck, in a sensible order (last on, first off).
      4. 

    4. Load in & build — on site, unpacked, positioned, rigged, cabled, powered.
      5. 

    5. Test — system check, line check, RF walk. Part 11 is entirely this step, because it's the one that decides whether the show is calm or awful.
      6. 

    6. Show — operate, monitor, stay alert, fix quietly.
      7. 

    7. Derig — down, coiled, cased, counted, loaded.
      8. 

    8. Return & check-in — back on the shelf, but only after it's been checked. Damaged or suspect kit gets flagged, not shelved.
      9. 

    

    Watch it
    Step 8 is where companies quietly lose money and reputation. A faulty mic that goes back on the shelf untested becomes someone's emergency in three weeks' time. Never shelve something you're not sure about — see §11.5 on quarantining.
    

    


    1.3 Who's who on site
    

    

    RoleAlso calledWhat they actually do
    


    Project ManagerPM, Account ManagerOwns the job commercially. Talks to the client. Decides what kit goes and what it costs. Usually not on site all day.
    

    Crew ChiefHead of Sound, Lead TechRuns the audio crew on site. Your boss for the day. Ask them before you change anything.
    

    Systems TechSystem Engineer, PA TechOwns the PA itself — design, rigging, amps, alignment, tuning. Specialist skill.
    

    FOH EngineerFront of House, "the mixer"Mixes what the audience hears. Sits in the room, not at the side.
    

    Monitor EngineerMons, MONMixes what the performers hear. Stage left/right, usually. Under more pressure than FOH.
    

    Stage TechPatch, Stage HandEverything on stage — mics, stands, DIs, patching, changeovers. Very often where you start.
    

    RF TechRadio TechWireless mics and IEMs, coordination, batteries. On big shows this is a full-time job.
    

    LX / LightingSparks, Board OpLighting. You'll share power, comms and cable routes with them, so be friendly. See Part 9.
    

    Video / AVVision, ScreensProjection, LED, cameras. You'll be feeding them audio or taking it from them constantly.
    

    Venue TechHouse Tech, Duty TechKnows where the power is, where the tie lines go, and what the noise limiter does. Be nice to this person. They can save your day.
    

    Production ManagerProd, PM (confusingly)Runs the whole event build across all departments. Their schedule is the schedule.
    

    Stage ManagerSMRuns what happens on stage during the show. Calls cues in theatre.
    

    

    Standard
    When you arrive on site, find out two things immediately: who's running audio today, and where the power is coming from. Everything else can wait five minutes.
    

    


    1.4 The shape of a show day
    

    

    PhaseWhat's happeningYour job in it
    


    Load inTrucks unloaded, kit into the roomMove things without damaging them or yourself. Keep routes clear.
    

    Build / rigPA up, stage set, FOH builtCable runs, positioning, assembling racks. Power first, then structure.
    

    PatchEverything connected to everythingWork off the patch list, methodically, in order.
    

    System checkPA proved and tunedUsually the systems tech's job — but you'll be walking the room and swapping cables.
    

    Line checkEvery input proved, one at a timeVery often your job. See §11.3. Get good at this and you'll get asked back.
    

    SoundcheckPerformers on stage, mixes builtStand by, fix things fast and quietly, take notes.
    

    DoorsAudience comes inEverything on stage stops. Look tidy. Be quiet.
    

    ShowThe bit everyone came forWatch, listen, be ready. Changeovers if there are support acts.
    

    DerigAll of it, backwards, fasterCoil properly even though it's 1am. Count everything.
    

    

    Watch it
    Doors is a hard line. Once the audience is in, no drilling, no shouting across the room, no wandering on stage in a hi-vis, no testing a wedge at volume. If something is broken at doors, you fix it silently or you fix it at the interval.
    

    


    1.5 The paperwork, and why it matters
    

    Every document below exists because someone once got it wrong without one. Learn to read all of them; learn to write the first three.
    

    

    Input list
    Numbered list of every source: 1 Kick In, 2 Kick Out, 3 Snare Top… It includes the mic type and whether it needs phantom or a DI. This is the single most useful bit of paper in live sound.
    

    Patch list
    Where each input physically lands — which stagebox, which socket, which console channel. Sometimes merged with the input list.
    

    Stage plan
    A top-down drawing of who stands where, where the wedges point, where the DIs and power are. Lets you build the stage before anyone arrives. Example below.
    

    Kit list
    What's going on the job. Your warehouse world. Check it against what's physically in the cases, not against what the system says.
    

    Tech spec / rider
    The artist's or client's requirements. Riders are aspirational; specs are contractual. Read them and flag anything you can't supply early.
    

    Schedule
    Times for load-in, soundcheck, doors, curfew. Curfew is usually a legal condition, not a suggestion.
    

    RAMS
    Risk Assessment & Method Statement. The safety paperwork for the job. See §13.7.
    

    Line check sheet
    Your own tick list for proving inputs. See Part 19.
    

    

    Standard
    Get a copy of the input list and stage plan on your phone before you leave the warehouse. Half of prep mistakes are "we didn't know they needed four DIs" and that's a five-second check.
    


    


    1.6 Site etiquette — the unwritten stuff
    

    This gets you rebooked more reliably than technical skill does, especially early on.
    

      

    • Don't touch what isn't yours. Never repatch, unplug, move or "tidy" someone else's kit without asking. Especially not a console. Especially not during a show.
      • 

    • Ask before you assume. "Do you want this here?" costs four seconds. Moving a stack twice costs twenty minutes.
      • 

    • Say when you don't know. Nobody minds "I've not done this before, show me once". Everyone minds finding out at line check that you guessed.
      • 

    • Wear black. Blacks on stage from soundcheck onwards, always in theatre. Steel toes on site.
      • 

    • Radio discipline. Listen before you talk, say who you are and who you want, keep it short, say "copy" not a monologue. Don't editorialise on the ring — everyone hears it, including the client.
      • 

    • Keep your area tidy as you go. Cable off walkways, cases stacked, tape off the floor. Tidy sites are safe sites and it's noticed.
      • 

    • Don't disappear. If you're going for a break or to the van, tell someone.
      • 

    • Eat and drink. Twelve-hour days will find you out. Water, food when catering's open, and don't let the first thing you consume all day be at wrap. The safety side of long days is §13.9.
      • 

    • Look busy is not the same as be busy. But when there's genuinely nothing to do, ask if anyone needs a hand rather than sitting on a case with your phone out.
      • 

    

    Also seen
    House style varies a lot on formality. A West End theatre and a festival stage have very different tolerances for chat, phones and clothing. Read the room in the first hour — watch what the experienced crew do and match it.
    

    


    1.7 Advancing a show
    

    "Advancing" is the work that happens before anyone loads a van — a call or email exchange with the client, venue or artist to find out what you're actually walking into. Early on, you probably won't run this call yourself, but you'll be handed its output (the input list, stage plan and schedule in §1.5) and you'll increasingly be the one someone asks "did anyone check X?" — so it's worth knowing what a good advance actually covers.
    

      

    1. Confirm the basics first — date, times, venue address, load-in access (loading bay, stairs, lift size, parking restrictions).
      2. 

    2. Get the input list and stage plan, even a rough one — see §1.5 for what good versions of these look like.
      3. 

    3. Ask what power is available and where it is relative to FOH and the stage — a venue that says "there's plenty of power" has usually not actually checked.
      4. 

    4. Ask what's already in the room — house PA, house console, existing rigging points — so you know what you're bringing versus what's provided. Assuming a "fully equipped venue" has what you need, without checking, is a common and expensive mistake.
      5. 

    5. Confirm who else is on site — other departments, their call times, whether you're sharing power or cable routes with them (Part 9).
      6. 

    6. Check any venue-specific restrictions — noise limits (§6.10), curfews, no-fly zones for rigging, restricted load-in hours.
      7. 

    7. Flag anything you can't supply, early — a rider requesting kit that's not in stock, a schedule that doesn't leave enough time to build safely. Raising this a week out is a conversation; raising it on the day is a crisis.
      8. 

    

    Standard
    A good advance answers questions before they become problems on site. If you're ever handed an advance that's clearly thin — missing power info, no stage plan, vague on access — it's worth flagging to whoever's running the job rather than just quietly hoping it works out.
    

    


    1.8 A day in the life — a worked example
    

    Everything above as separate topics can feel disconnected from what a real day actually looks like. Here's one, stitched together, with links back to where each part is properly explained.
    

    

    06:30
    Arrive at the warehouse. Check the job sheet against what's been pulled overnight — kit list versus what's actually in the cases (§1.2). Spot a DI missing from the count; grab a spare rather than assuming it'll turn up.
    

    07:15
    Load the van in reverse order of need — last on, first off (§19.3). Paperwork — RAMS, input list, contact numbers — goes in your bag, not just on a shared drive.
    

    08:30
    Arrive on site. First two questions: who's running audio today, and where's the power coming from (§1.3). Meet the LX crew chief while you're at it — you'll be sharing a cable route with them later (§9.5).
    

    09:00–11:30
    Build: PA positioned and rigged, stage cabled, console patched to match the patch list. A DI you're handed crackles when you wiggle the cable — swap it and quarantine the faulty one rather than fighting it mid-build (§11.5).
    

    12:00
    Line check, patch order, one input at a time, ticking off as you go (§11.3). Channel 14 is silent — gain's at zero, not actually faulty. Channel 22 stays quiet after that's fixed — swap the cable, that clears it (§12.9).
    

    13:30
    Wireless proving — walk every pack through where the performers will actually stand, watching the RF meter, not just checking it makes a sound at all (§5.8).
    

    15:00
    Soundcheck. Monitor requests come fast — a wedge with nothing in it turns out to be a pre-fade aux with the fader down, not a dead speaker (§15.6).
    

    17:45
    Doors. Everything on stage stops being adjusted out loud from this point (§1.4). A last-minute buzz turns out to be a cable now running parallel to a lighting run that wasn't there this morning — move it, problem gone (§9.2).
    

    20:00–22:30
    Show. Watch, listen, fix quietly, take notes for tomorrow.
    

    23:00
    Derig — coiled properly even though it's late, everything counted before it leaves the building, the faulty DI from this morning handed in properly flagged, not just shelved (§19.7).
    

    

    Nothing in that day was exotic. It was the fundamentals, applied in order, under a bit of time pressure — which is really what most of this book is training you for.
    

    


    1.9 The different worlds of event audio
    

    "Events" is one job title covering genuinely different working cultures. The core skills — signal flow, patching, line check — carry across all of them; what changes is the pace, the paperwork, and how much room there is to improvise. Knowing which world a job sits in tells you what to expect before you arrive.
    

    

    Corporate & conference
    AGMs, product launches, awards dinners, panel discussions. Tight running order, radio mics on delegates who've never worn one, playback cues to the second, high client visibility. Formal dress, minimal visible cable, very low tolerance for anything audible going wrong mid-speech.
    

    Live music & touring
    Bands, one-off gigs, support-band changeovers. Faster, noisier build; more paperwork upfront (rider, stage plan, input list) but less formality on site than corporate work.
    

    Theatre
    A fixed, repeatable run rather than a one-off show. Cue-driven, careful radio mic changeovers between cast members, and stricter backstage discipline than a touring gig — see the "wear black" habit in §1.6.
    

    Outdoor & festival
    Weather, generators, longer cable runs, a licensing-condition noise limit that's actively enforced on-site (§6.10), and more genuine improvisation than any of the above — less shelter for kit, people or plans.
    

    Private parties & weddings
    Often your first paid solo booking. No producer, no crew hierarchy — you're frequently the only production person on site. See §10.9 for what's different.
    

    

    Standard
    Ask which of these a job sits in before you leave the warehouse — it changes what to wear, how much paperwork to expect, and how much slack there is if the build runs late.
    

    


    1.10 The part nobody puts in a manual
    

    Every technical manual, including this one, can make it sound like the job is only ever a sequence of correct actions. It isn't. Some of it is standing next to someone who's done this for fifteen years, understanding about a third of what they just said on the radio, and trying not to let it show. That feeling is completely normal — it happens to nearly everyone at some point, however experienced they look now — and it's worth a page of its own rather than pretending it away.
    

    Standard
    Everyone currently confident on a stagebox once didn't know what a stagebox was. The gap you can see between yourself and an experienced tech is real, but it's a gap of reps, not of ability — and it closes faster than it feels like it will.
    

    

    Why this job makes it louder than most
    The mistakes are audible, the audience is real, and jargon flies past on the radio fast enough that you can't always ask what something meant in the moment. That combination makes ordinary new-job nerves feel bigger here than in a quieter job where a slow week goes unnoticed.
    

    The comparison that isn't fair
    Measuring your month three against someone else's year ten is a rigged comparison — they've had the ten years of reps you haven't had yet. A fairer one is your month three against your own month one.
    

    In the moment
    Narrow the job down to the next physical action, not the evaluation. "Coil this cable" is manageable; "am I good enough to be here" isn't a question you can usefully answer mid-show. §12.7's approach to asking for help works the same way — one small, specific action beats one large, vague worry.
    

    After a mistake
    What almost always actually happens: someone notices, it gets quietly fixed, and within a day nobody but you remembers it. What it feels like happens: everyone clocked it and is silently judging you. The second one is very rarely true. Own it briefly, fix what's yours to fix, and let the moment end — dwelling on it on site costs you the next task's attention, which is the thing actually in your control.
    

    Write it down instead of carrying it
    The learning log exists partly for this. A specific, three-minute note turns a vague bad feeling about a shift into a concrete, fixable thing — and concrete things are much easier to stop worrying about than vague ones.
    

    

    Watch it
    Normal nerves settle with reps. If a job is leaving you dreading it, not sleeping, or feeling genuinely low well beyond the shift itself, that's no longer just new-job nerves, and it's worth talking to someone about — a GP, or the British Association for Performing Arts Medicine (BAPAM), a UK charity supporting the health of people working in live events and performance, crew included, not just performers. Pushing through in silence isn't the professional option; asking for help is — the same standard §17.6 already sets for asking for more responsibility applies just as well to asking for support.
    

    


    


    

    PART 2
    Audio essentials
    The signal-flow mental model everything else hangs on. Learn this properly before chasing specialist knowledge.
    

    


    2.1 The chain, start to finish
    

    Every single audio system, from a lectern in a meeting room to a stadium, is this:
    

    SOURCE          a voice, a guitar amp, a laptop
   ↓
TRANSDUCER      microphone / DI  — turns sound or an instrument signal into a small electrical one
   ↓
PREAMP          console input — brings that tiny signal up to a usable working level
   ↓
PROCESSING      EQ, dynamics, effects, routing, mixing
   ↓
AMPLIFIER       power amp or the amp inside an active speaker
   ↓
TRANSDUCER      loudspeaker — turns electricity back into sound
   ↓
EARS            the only part of the system that actually matters
    


    When something doesn't work, you are always asking one question: where along this chain did it stop? That's it. That's fault-finding (Part 12). Everything else is detail.
    

    Standard
    Learn to picture the chain physically — "the signal is currently in that XLR, going into socket 4 of that stagebox, arriving on channel 4 of the console". People who can do this fix things in seconds. People who can't press buttons hopefully.
    

    


    2.2 Signal levels — the four worlds
    

    Audio signals exist at wildly different strengths, and mixing them up is the single most common source of "it sounds terrible" and occasionally "it's now on fire".
    

    

    LevelRough voltageWhere you meet itConnector
    


    Mic level~1–10 mVMicrophone output. Tiny. Needs a preamp.XLR
    

    Instrument level~10–100 mVGuitar/bass pickup. Also high impedance — needs a DI.TS jack
    

    Line level~0.3–1.5 VLaptops, mixers, playback, processors. The standard "carrying" level.XLR / TRS / RCA
    

    Speaker level10–100+ VAmp output to a passive speaker. Genuinely dangerous to inputs.speakON
    

    

    Watch it
    Plugging a speaker output into an input destroys the input. This is why speaker connections are speakON and not jack — the connector shape is a safety feature. If you find a passive speaker wired with a jack, treat it as a fault to be fixed, not a quirk.
    

    Also seen
    Older passive wedges and some backline still use 1/4" jack for speaker connections, and some cheap install gear uses bare-wire terminals. They exist, they work, they're just easier to get wrong. If you're handed one, label it clearly.
    

    Open the level converter → dBu, dBV and volts, in Support with the rest of the calculators.
    


    


    2.3 Balanced vs unbalanced, and why XLR won
    

    Unbalanced (a guitar lead, an RCA, a 3.5mm jack) carries the signal on one conductor with a shield around it. Any interference the cable picks up along the way gets added to the signal. Fine for two metres, hopeless for twenty.
    

    Balanced (XLR, TRS) carries the same signal twice — once normal, once polarity-flipped — plus a shield. At the far end, the receiving device flips one back and adds them together. The wanted signal doubles; anything picked up equally by both wires cancels out. This is called common-mode rejection, and it's why you can run a balanced mic line 100 m past a dimmer rack and still get clean audio.
    

    

    Practical rule
    Balanced for anything long or anything mic level. Unbalanced only for short runs of line-level, and get it onto a DI as soon as you can.
    

    Pinout
    XLR pin 1 = screen/earth, pin 2 = hot (+), pin 3 = cold (−). Memorable as "one is ground, two is hot". This is the AES standard and effectively universal now.
    

    Direction
    Signal flows out of male pins and into female sockets. So a cable has a female end that goes on the source, and a male end that goes into the destination. "Female follows the source" is one way to remember it.
    

    


    Also seen
    Some vintage gear (older Japanese consoles, some 70s/80s equipment) is wired pin 3 hot. If you meet a polarity problem you can't explain on one specific old box, this is why. Modern kit is pin 2 hot without exception.
    

    


    2.4 Gain vs volume vs trim vs fader
    

    People use these interchangeably and it causes endless confusion. They are not the same control.
    

    

    Gain / Trim
    At the input. Sets how much the preamp amplifies the incoming signal to bring it to a healthy internal working level. Set once, correctly, then mostly leave alone. Too little = noise. Too much = distortion.
    

    Fader
    After the processing. Sets how much of that channel goes into the mix. This is your musical control — move it constantly.
    

    Volume / Master
    At the output. How loud the whole thing is.
    

    

    The distinction matters because turning up the wrong one has completely different consequences. If a vocal is too quiet, the fader is almost always the answer. If a vocal is quiet and hissy, the gain was set too low. If it's distorting even with the fader down, the gain is too high — the damage already happened at the input.
    

    


    2.5 Gain structure & headroom
    

    This is the concept that separates people whose systems sound clean from people whose systems sound rough, and it's genuinely simple: at every stage of the chain, the signal should be comfortably in the middle of what that stage can handle.
    

    Too low and you're amplifying noise later on to compensate. Too high and you clip. The space between your normal level and the point of clipping is headroom, and you want plenty of it because live sources are unpredictable — the singer who soundchecked politely will be twice as loud with an audience in.
    

    Standard
    On a digital console, aim your input gain so normal programme material sits around −18 dBFS average, peaking to maybe −10 dBFS. That leaves 10–18 dB of headroom for surprises. On most desks that's the boundary between the green and the yellow on the meter. If you're regularly touching red, you've gained it too hot.
    


    Also seen
    Plenty of engineers gain hotter than that — chasing the sound of a preamp being driven, or working on kit where the noise floor is worse than the clipping. And analogue desks are a different game entirely: there, 0 VU is your target and the meters mean something different. The −18 dBFS figure is a digital-console rule of thumb, not a law.
    

    Go deeper
    Search "gain staging live sound" and read anything from Rational Acoustics or ProSoundWeb. It's a concept worth understanding rather than memorising — see §18.4.
    

    


    2.6 Phantom power (+48 V)
    

    Condenser mics and active DI boxes need power to work. Rather than run a separate supply, the console sends 48 V DC up the same XLR cable that the audio comes back down — equally on pins 2 and 3, referenced to pin 1. Because it's identical on both signal wires, the balanced input ignores it.
    

    

    DeviceNeeds phantom?Harmed by phantom?
    


    Dynamic mic (SM58, SM57…)NoNo — safe, just pointless
    

    Condenser micYesNo
    

    Active DI boxYesNo
    

    Passive DI boxNoNo
    

    Ribbon micUsually noPotentially yes — can destroy the ribbon
    

    Wireless receiver outputNoGenerally no, but check
    

    Line output from other gearNoUsually no if balanced; can be bad if unbalanced
    

    

    Watch it
    Three habits worth building. One: mute the channel before switching phantom on or off — the thump is loud and can damage drivers. Two: never plug or unplug a mic with phantom live on that channel, for the same reason. Three: on desks with a single global phantom switch for a whole rack, check what else is plugged in before you hit it. Ribbon mics and vintage gear are the casualties.
    

    Also seen
    Some engineers just leave phantom on across the board permanently on modern digital desks, on the basis that nothing in a standard hire stock is harmed by it. It's a defensible position on a rock gig with no ribbons. It's a bad habit to learn as a default, because eventually you'll meet a ribbon or a piece of vintage kit.
    

    


    2.7 Impedance, briefly
    

    Impedance is resistance to an AC signal, measured in ohms (Ω). You mostly need three facts:
    

      

    • Mic inputs are low impedance and expect a low-impedance source. Mics are typically 150–600 Ω, inputs around 1.5–3 kΩ. This mismatch is deliberate — it's called bridging and it's correct.
      • 

    • Instrument pickups are high impedance. Plug a guitar straight into a mic input and it'll sound thin and lifeless because the input loads the pickup down. That's what a DI box is for (§3.9).
      • 

    • Speakers have impedance too — usually 4, 8 or 16 Ω. This matters when you're wiring multiple passive speakers to one amp channel: two 8 Ω boxes in parallel make a 4 Ω load, which draws more current from the amp. Go too low and the amp overheats or shuts down. Modern active boxes make this a non-issue, which is one reason they took over.
      • 

    

    


    2.8 Polarity vs phase
    

    Used interchangeably in conversation; technically different, and the difference occasionally matters.
    

    

    Polarity
    Whether the waveform is the right way up. Flipping it inverts the whole signal at all frequencies. The Ø button on your console does this. Instant, frequency-independent.
    

    Phase
    A time relationship between two signals. Because a fixed time delay is a different fraction of a cycle at different frequencies, phase problems are frequency-dependent — which is why two mics on the same source at different distances sound hollow, not just quiet.
    

    

    Practically: if two mics on the same source sound thin and weedy together but fine alone, try the polarity flip on one. If it gets fuller, you had a polarity problem. If it changes but doesn't fix it, you've got a distance/timing problem and the answer is moving a mic, not pressing a button.
    

    Standard
    Classic cases where you'll reach for the polarity button: snare top vs snare bottom (bottom mic almost always gets flipped), kick in vs kick out, a guitar cab mic'd front and back, and DI vs mic on the same bass rig.
    

    


    2.9 Analogue, digital, and the clock
    

    Digital audio samples the waveform many thousands of times a second and stores each sample as a number.
    

    

    Sample rate
    How many snapshots per second. 48 kHz is the live/video standard; 44.1 kHz is the CD/music standard; 96 kHz exists and is rarely worth the I/O cost live. Everything on one network must agree.
    

    Bit depth
    How precisely each snapshot is measured. 24-bit is standard and gives you a huge dynamic range. This is why digital headroom is generous — but clipping is still absolute and ugly.
    

    Latency
    The delay caused by converting, processing and transporting. A few milliseconds is invisible; stack up enough conversions and processors and musicians start to notice, especially on in-ears.
    

    Clock (word clock)
    Every digital device must agree on exactly when a sample happens. One device is the master and the rest follow. "Word clock" is the actual term printed on converters and consoles for this — a dedicated clock signal, or a setting, telling a device whose timing to follow. Get this wrong and you get clicks, pops, or dropouts.
    

    

    Watch it
    Two clock masters on one network is a classic and infuriating fault — intermittent ticking that comes and goes. When you build a digital system, decide what the clock master is (usually the console, or a dedicated clock source) and check every other device is set to follow. See §8.2 for how this looks in Dante Controller.
    

    


    2.10 Decibels, without the maths
    

    The dB is a ratio, not a fixed amount, which is why it always has a suffix telling you what it's a ratio to.
    

    

    UnitReferenceUsed for
    


    dB SPLThreshold of hearingActual loudness in the air. What a sound level meter reads.
    

    dBu0.775 VAnalogue signal level. "+4 dBu" is pro line level.
    

    dBV1 VConsumer line level, "−10 dBV". Quieter than pro.
    

    dBFSDigital full scaleDigital metering. 0 dBFS is the ceiling — you cannot go above it.
    

    dBA / dBCWeighted SPLNoise limits. A-weighting ignores bass, C-weighting includes it.
    

    

    Rules of thumb worth memorising
    

      

    • +3 dB = double the power. Barely audible as a change.
      • 

    • +6 dB = double the voltage. Clearly audible.
      • 

    • +10 dB = roughly twice as loud to a human. Needs ten times the power.
      • 

    • Double the distance = −6 dB from a point source. The inverse square law. This is why the front row is deafened while the back is quiet, and why line arrays and delay stacks exist.
      • 

    • Doubling the number of identical sources = +3 dB (if uncorrelated) or +6 dB (if perfectly correlated, e.g. coupled subs).
      • 

    

    


    2.11 What lives where — frequency crib
    

    Learn these ranges and EQ stops being guesswork. Human hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the top end goes first with age and exposure.
    

    

    RangeNameWhat's thereToo much sounds…
    


    20–60 HzSub-bassFelt more than heard. Kick body, synth subs, rumble.Muddy, uncontrolled, boomy
    

    60–250 HzBassFundamental of bass guitar, kick punch, male voice weightBoomy, woolly
    

    250–500 HzLow midWarmth — and the classic "mud" zoneBoxy, congested
    

    500 Hz–2 kHzMidBody and intelligibility of most instruments; vocal fundamentalsHonky, nasal, telephone-ish
    

    2–4 kHzUpper midConsonants, attack, presence. The ear is most sensitive here.Harsh, fatiguing, shouty
    

    4–8 kHzPresenceClarity, definition, sibilance startsSibilant, piercing
    

    8–20 kHzAir / brillianceSparkle, cymbal shimmer, sense of spaceBrittle, hissy
    

    

    Standard
    When something sounds wrong, the pro move is almost always cut, don't boost. Find the offending frequency by boosting a narrow band and sweeping until it gets worse, then cut there instead. Subtractive EQ keeps headroom and sounds more natural.
    

    Go deeper
    Ear training is the highest-leverage thing you can do for your mixing. Free browser tools like SoundGym's free trainers or the "Train Your Ears" style EQ quizzes get you recognising frequencies within a few weeks of ten-minute sessions. See §18.6.
    

    


    


    

    PART 3
    Connections, cables & power
    The everyday physical layer of the job—and where a large share of faults begin.
    

    


    3.1 XLR — the workhorse
    

    Three-pin, latching, balanced, and the connector that carries almost all mic and line audio in live sound.
    

    

    Pin 1
    Screen / earth / shield
    

    Pin 2
    Hot (+), in-phase signal
    

    Pin 3
    Cold (−), inverted signal
    

    

    Brands you'll handle: Neutrik (the good stuff — the X-series with the coloured ring, and the chunky NC3 range), Amphenol, Switchcraft, and various no-brand ones that are why the cable failed. Neutrik connectors are worth learning to strip and solder; it's the single most useful practical skill you can pick up in a warehouse.
    

    Standard
    Cable lengths in most UK hire stock are colour-coded or ring-coded by length — commonly 1 m, 3 m, 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 30 m. Learn your company's system on day one; grabbing the right length first time is a superpower on a build.
    

    Also seen
    Five-pin XLR is used for DMX lighting control (§9.7) and for some dual-channel headset/intercom applications. Four-pin XLR is standard for single-ear intercom headsets. Three-pin DMX exists on cheap fixtures and is a constant source of "why won't this talk to that" — you'll need turnarounds.
    

    Watch it
    Never use a mic cable for DMX or DMX cable for audio as a matter of habit. DMX is impedance-matched at 120 Ω; mic cable isn't built as a matched transmission line at all, and while swapping them usually works over short runs, it causes flickering fixtures and intermittent faults over long ones. The fact that the connector fits doesn't mean the cable is right.
    

    


    3.2 Jacks — TS, TRS, TRRS
    

    

    TypeContactsCarriesYou'll see it on
    


    TS (mono jack)Tip, SleeveOne unbalanced signalGuitar leads, instrument cables, some speaker cables (legacy)
    

    TRS (stereo jack)Tip, Ring, SleeveEither one balanced signal or two unbalanced (L/R)Balanced line I/O, headphones, insert points
    

    TRRSTip, Ring, Ring, SleeveStereo + mic (headset)Phones, laptops, consumer headsets
    

    

    The ambiguity of TRS is the thing to internalise: the same connector means two completely different things depending on the socket. A TRS in a headphone socket is stereo unbalanced. A TRS in a console line input is mono balanced. An "insert cable" is TRS at one end splitting to two TS — send and return — for patching an outboard processor into a channel.
    

    Watch it
    3.5 mm minijack is the most fragile connector you'll deal with and it will be the thing feeding the client's laptop into your system on a corporate job. Always use a DI box rather than a long minijack-to-XLR lead, always tape the connector to the laptop or table so a knocked cable doesn't yank the socket out, and always carry spares. Consider it a consumable.
    

    


    3.3 speakON — and why speaker cable is different
    

    Neutrik speakON is the standard for connecting amplifiers to passive speakers. It twists to lock, the contacts are shrouded so you can't touch live terminals, and it handles serious current.
    

    

    NL2
    Two poles (+1/−1). One channel.
    

    NL4
    Four poles (+1/−1/+2/−2). Two channels down one cable — used for bi-amped boxes, or for a top and a sub, or to link through. Part numbers, NLT4 (STX), testing and faults: §3.12.
    

    NL8
    Eight poles. Multi-way, mostly on line array and larger systems.
    

    

    Speaker cable is not signal cable. It's unshielded, heavy-gauge (typically 2.5 mm² or 4 mm² for long runs) because it's carrying real current. Using thin cable on a long run loses power and damping — the bass goes soft. Using signal cable will, at best, sound bad; at worst it melts.
    

    Open the speaker cable loss estimator → Is this run thin enough over this distance to matter.
    

    Watch it
    An NL4 will physically plug into an NL8 socket and vice versa in some combinations, and a two-pole cable in a four-pole socket may give you nothing, or may give you the wrong driver. If a top is silent but the sub works, check you haven't got a cable wired on 2+/2− going into a box expecting 1+/1−. Label your speaker cables by pinout, not just length.
    


    


    3.4 The consumer connectors you'll be handed
    

      

    • RCA / phono — unbalanced, colour-coded red (right) and white or black (left). DJ mixers, CDJs, domestic gear. Short runs only, into a DI.
      • 

    • 3.5 mm minijack — laptops, phones. See the warning above.
      • 

    • USB-C / Lightning — increasingly the only audio output on a modern laptop or phone. Carry adapters; carry spares of the adapters.
      • 

    • HDMI — carries audio as well as video. On corporate jobs the client's audio often arrives embedded in HDMI and has to be de-embedded. Know who owns that box.
      • 

    • Bluetooth — will be requested. It's laggy, lossy and drops out. Fine for background music before doors, never for anything that matters.
      • 

    

    Standard
    On any corporate or conference job, build a "presenter's kit" that lives in a small case: 3.5 mm to XLR DI, USB-C and Lightning adapters, HDMI de-embedder if you have one, gaffa, and a couple of spare leads. You will use it on every single job.
    

    


    3.5 Multicores, looms, stageboxes
    

    Rather than run 32 individual XLRs from stage to FOH, you run one thick cable containing all of them.
    

    

    Multicore / snake
    The cable itself. UK tends to say "multicore", US says "snake".
    

    Stagebox
    The metal box at the stage end with all the sockets in it, numbered.
    

    Fan-out / tails
    The bunch of individual connectors at the other end.
    

    Sends and returns
    A multicore usually carries inputs one way and a few outputs (for wedges, or a feed to the stage) the other. Described as e.g. "32/8" — 32 in, 8 out.
    

    Digital stagebox
    The modern version: converters at the stage end, one Cat5e or fibre run back to the console. Far lighter and higher channel count. See §3.7.
    

    

    Standard
    Always run the multicore first, before anything else is cabled, and always run it where it won't be walked on, driven over or need to be moved. Once it's down and taped, it stays down. Leave a service loop at both ends so you can reposition the console a metre without repulling the whole run.
    

    


    3.6 Network cable — now core audio infrastructure
    

    A huge amount of modern live audio travels over ordinary-looking network cable, which means network faults are now audio faults.
    

      

    • Cat5e is adequate for most audio networking; Cat6 and Cat6a give more margin. Use shielded (STP/FTP) for touring — the electrical environment is hostile.
      • 

    • etherCON is Neutrik's ruggedised housing around a standard RJ45. It latches, it survives being trodden on, and it's what you should use on site. A bare RJ45 on a floor is a fault waiting to happen.
      • 

    • 100 m is the hard limit for copper Ethernet, per hop. Beyond that you need a switch in the middle or fibre.
      • 

    • Fibre (usually with opticalCON connectors) for long runs, and it's immune to electrical interference. Treat it gently — the minimum bend radius is real and a kinked fibre is a dead fibre.
      • 

    

    Watch it
    Network cable does not like being coiled tightly, crushed by a case wheel, or kinked. It'll often still pass a link light while dropping packets — which sounds like intermittent clicks and dropouts and is a nightmare to trace. If you suspect a Cat5 run, swap it before you spend an hour in software.
    

    


    3.7 Digital audio transports — the alphabet soup
    

    

    NameWhoRuns onNotes
    


    DanteAudinateStandard EthernetThe dominant standard. Routes freely between any devices on the network. Learn this one properly — §8.2.
    

    AES50Klark Teknik / Behringer / MidasCat5e, point to pointWhat X32/M32/Wing use for their stageboxes. Simple, fixed, cheap. Not a routable network.
    

    MADIAES standardCoax or optical64 channels, point to point, very well established. Common as a link between big systems and recording rigs.
    

    AES3 / AES-EBUAES standardXLR (110 Ω)Two channels of digital audio down one XLR. Looks like an audio cable, isn't.
    

    AVB / MilanIEEE / AvnuSpecial AVB switchesUsed by Avid, d&b, L-Acoustics, Meyer. Deterministic and robust; needs compatible switches.
    

    ADATAlesisOptical "lightpipe"8 channels at 48 kHz. Legacy but still all over studios and small rigs.
    

    Optocore / SoundGrid / A-NetVariousFibre / EthernetManufacturer-specific. You'll meet them on specific rigs and read specific manuals.
    

    

    Go deeper
    Audinate run free online Dante certification (Levels 1–3). Level 1 takes an afternoon and is genuinely the best-value qualification in live audio right now — it's free, it's recognised, and it directly makes you more employable. Do it. Link in §18.3.
    

    Also seen
    PoE (Power over Ethernet) carries power down the same cable as the network data, so a switch or an inline injector can run a device — a small stagebox, an access point, a networked speaker or a control panel — without a separate mains lead. Convenient for small, remote or awkward-to-power devices; not something you'd rely on for anything drawing serious current. Check a device's PoE class before assuming a given switch port can actually supply enough of it.
    

    


    3.8 Power
    

    You will not be wiring distros as a junior, but you must understand what you're plugging into.
    

    

    13 A
    Standard UK three-pin plug. Fine for consoles, small racks, active speakers.
    

    16 A ceeform
    Blue round industrial connector. The event-industry standard for single-phase distribution.
    

    32 A ceeform
    Bigger blue one. Feeds distros and bigger amp racks.
    

    Three-phase (63 A / 125 A)
    Red ceeform. Feeds the whole event. Three live legs — and balancing loads across them is a skilled job. Not yours yet.
    

    IEC
    The kettle-lead connector on the back of nearly everything. C13/C14 is standard; C19/C20 is the bigger high-current version on amps.
    

    powerCON / powerCON TRUE1
    Neutrik locking mains connectors. TRUE1 is the one you can safely connect and disconnect under load. Blue in, white out — the convention is input is grey/blue, output is white.
    

    

    Watch it
    Never remove or defeat an earth pin to solve a hum problem. Ever. It's the thing that stops a fault killing someone. If you have an earth loop, fix it properly with a DI box's ground lift or an isolating transformer — §12.3. There is no situation in which lifting mains earth is acceptable, and anyone who tells you otherwise is dangerous.
    

    Standard
    Get all audio on the same power source where possible — same distro, same phase. Sharing a supply with lighting dimmers, LED walls or motors is the most common cause of buzz on a job. If you must share, ask for a separate audio supply early, before the power is committed.
    

    Go deeper
    PAT — Portable Appliance Testing — is a routine warehouse task and an easy qualification to pick up. If your company does it in-house, ask to be trained. It makes you more useful immediately and it's a genuine line on a CV. The distribution itself — generators, distros, RCD protection, cable runs — is designed and signed off against BS 7909, the industry code of practice for temporary electrical systems at events. You won't be the one designing it, but knowing the name means you understand why a distro on a job looks the way it does, and why an electrician can point at a specific requirement rather than just "that's how we do it". See §18.8.
    

    Also seen
    Increasingly, generators run on HVO — hydrotreated vegetable oil — instead of red diesel. It's a drop-in fuel for most modern diesel generators (no engine modification), burns with substantially lower net carbon and particulate output, and is turning up more often on festival and touring power specs as production companies chase sustainability targets. You'll just be told to fuel from whichever drum you're handed, but it's worth knowing why it might not smell like ordinary diesel. Events chasing that reputation may be seeking or holding certification from A Greener Future (formerly A Greener Festival), which audits events against environmental standards — generator fuel and power efficiency is one of the things it looks at.
    

    


    3.9 DI boxes
    

    A DI (Direct Injection) box does three jobs: converts unbalanced to balanced, converts high impedance to low impedance, and often provides a ground lift to break earth loops. It's the universal adapter of live sound.
    

    

    TypePowered?Best forCommon models
    


    PassiveNoHot sources — active basses, keyboards, line outputsRadial ProDI, Radial JDI, Behringer DI400P
    

    ActivePhantom or batteryWeak sources — passive basses, acoustic guitar pickupsBSS AR-133, Klark Teknik DN100, Radial J48, Countryman Type 85
    

    StereoEitherLaptops, keyboards, playbackRadial ProD2, Behringer DI20
    

    Media / AV DIUsually active3.5 mm and RCA sources on corporate jobsRadial ProAV2, Radial StageBug
    

    

    Standard
    Ground lift off by default; flip it on only if you have a hum. It's a fault-finding tool, not a setting. And check what the DI's "thru" socket is for — it passes the unbalanced signal on to the performer's amp so they can use their own rig as well as feeding your system.
    

    


    3.10 Cable care — coiling, labelling, storage
    

    You already do a lot of this, so this is mostly the why.
    

    Over-under coiling
    

    The correct way to coil any cable: alternate loops, one twisted one way and the next the other. The cable stores with no net twist and pays out flat with a straight pull. The wrong way — winding it all the same direction round your elbow — builds a twist into the cable every single coil, which over months breaks the conductors inside and turns a good cable into an intermittent one.
    

    Standard
    Over-under, every time, and coil in the cable's natural loop size. Tie with the cable's own velcro or a proper cable tie — never a knot in the cable itself, and never a tight zip tie which crushes the jacket.
    

    Also seen
    Some people figure-of-eight long runs instead, and some theatre departments coil onto drums for permanent installs. Both are fine. What's not fine is elbow-winding, and you'll see people do it constantly.
    

    Other habits
    

      

    • Pull from the connector's cable, never the connector. The strain relief exists but it's not infinite.
      • 

    • Never pull a cable round a sharp corner under tension.
      • 

    • Label both ends if it's part of a system. Numbered heatshrink or a wrap of LTC (paper tape) with a Sharpie.
      • 

    • Don't run cable over doorways at head height, don't tape it across fire exits, and get it out of walkways or under a ramp.
      • 

    • Store coiled and hung, not in a heap in the bottom of a case where the weight crushes the ones underneath.
      • 

    

    


    3.11 How cables actually fail
    

    

    SymptomLikely causeTest
    


    Dead silentBroken conductor, usually at the connectorCable tester, or swap
    

    Intermittent — cuts in and outCracked solder joint or fatigued conductor at the strain reliefWiggle test at each end while it's live
    

    Quiet and hummyOne leg down — pin 2 or 3 broken, so the balance is goneCable tester will show it; ear will suspect it
    

    Buzz that changes when you touch itBroken screen (pin 1)Cable tester
    

    Crackling when movedDirty or loose contactsContact cleaner, or bin it
    

    

    Standard
    A cable tester (Behringer CT100, Rolls, Whirlwind Tester) is cheap and pays for itself in one avoided show. But the wiggle test catches things a static tester misses — plug it in, pass signal, and flex the cable hard at both connectors. Intermittents live in that last 50 mm.
    

    


    3.12 NL4 & NLT4 speaker cables — the full picture
    

    On the shelf, "an NL4" and "an NLT4" usually mean the same thing: a four-pole speakON speaker cable. The letters are Neutrik part numbers for the connector on the end, and once you can read them you know what a cable will and won't do before you've uncoiled it.
    

    Reading the part numbers
    

    

    PartWhat it isWhere you'll see it
    


    NL4MP / NL4MPRChassis socket — the square-flanged one fixed to a panelAmp outputs, speaker input and link sockets
    

    NL4FX / NL4FCStandard cable connector, plastic body. Plugs into a chassis socketThe end of most install and older hire cables
    

    NLT4FX / NLT4FXX-BAGThe STX heavy-duty, all-metal version of the same cable connector. Same four pins, same socket, tougher and higher-ratedTouring and rental stock — this is what "NLT4" on a label means
    

    NLT4MX / NLT4MXXSTX male cable connector. Lets one cable plug straight into anotherExtension cables (NLT4 female one end, NLT4 male the other)
    

    NL4MMXInline coupler — joins two ordinary NL4FX cable endsFault kit, for lengthening a run
    

    NL2FXTwo-pole cable connector. Fits a four-pole socket but only connects pins 1+/1−Older cables — and a classic trap
    

    

    What the four poles carry
    

    

    PinsGeneral useOn d&b systems (see §6.17)
    


    1+ / 1−The first (or only) channelTops and full-range boxes · the LF in 2-way active · channel A or C
    

    2+ / 2−A second channel, or a link through to the next boxSubs in Mix TOP/SUB · the HF in 2-way active · channel B or D
    

    

    So a four-core NL4 can carry two separate amp channels down one cable — which is exactly how a d&b amp feeds a top and a sub, or the two halves of an actively driven box, from one connector. A two-core cable on NL4 ends carries only pins 1, and anything that needed pins 2 goes silent.
    

    How to connect and release one
    

      

    1. Mute first. Mute the amp channel (or have it in standby) before you plug or unplug. Speaker level is real voltage and current — breaking it under load arcs across the contacts and pits them, and can pop a driver.
      2. 

    2. Line up the key — the connector only goes in one way. Push it fully home; don't force it.
      3. 

    3. Twist clockwise about a quarter turn until it latches with a click. If there was no click, it isn't locked.
      4. 

    4. Tug-test gently on the connector body, not the cable. A locked speakON doesn't move.
      5. 

    5. To release: pull back the latch (the sliding tab on the connector), twist anticlockwise, then pull the body straight out. Never yank the cable.
      6. 

    

    Checking and testing
    

      

    • Look before every job: strain relief (the chuck at the back) tight, no copper or inner insulation showing, latch springs back, body not cracked, pins straight, nothing rattling inside.
      • 

    • Test, don't trust: put every speaker cable through a speakON-capable cable tester at prep. You want all four poles continuous end to end and no shorts between any of them — a short across a speaker line is a dead short on the amp.
      • 

    • With only a meter: each core end-to-end should read a fraction of an ohm on a normal-length cable; between any two different cores it should read open (no continuity).
      • 

    • Label by type, not just length: "4-core 2.5 mm² 20 m" tells the next person whether this cable will carry a sub on pins 2. Many companies colour-code 2-core vs 4-core — learn yours.
      • 

    

    

    4 × 2.5 mm²
    The everyday four-core speaker cable.
    

    4 × 4 mm²
    For longer runs, where thin cable would lose level and control of the bass (the cable loss estimator shows when it starts to matter).
    

    8-core + NL8
    Multicore runs to arrays — four channels on one cable, broken out to NL4s at the far end with a breakout box or fan.
    

    

    

    SymptomLikely causeTest
    


    Box dead silentConnector not latched, broken core, or a 2-core cable where pins 2 were neededRe-seat and lock, then swap for a known-good 4-core
    

    Cuts in and out, crackles when movedConnector a quarter-turn short of locked, worn contacts, conductor broken at the strain reliefLock it; wiggle the cable at each end with low-level signal; swap
    

    Sub silent, top fine (or the reverse)Cable only carries pins 1, or the box is on the wrong amp connector for the modeCheck the cable is 4-core and on the right output — §6.19
    

    Amp channel trips or protects as soon as signal arrivesShort circuit in cable or connectorUnplug the cable at the box; if the fault stays, it's the cable — quarantine it
    

    Contacts look burnt or blackenedPlugged or unplugged under load, or a loose connection running hotTake it out of service (§11.5)
    

    

    Watch it
    Don't re-terminate speakON on site unless you're trained, authorised and have the right parts. A wrongly wired NL4 — pins 1 and 2 swapped, or a core shorted — can send a sub feed into a top's HF section, or put a dead short across an amp channel. Swap in a known-good cable, label the bad one, and repair it properly back at base.
    

    Also seen
    Older German and touring stock sometimes uses EP5 (or EP4/EP6) connectors instead of speakON, and some d&b amps came in EP5 versions. They aren't interchangeable with NL4 without an adapter, and the pin numbering is different — check the amp's label before using one.
    

    


    


    

    PART 4
    Microphones & stage capture
    What you will handle most often, how it behaves, and how to place and protect it.
    

    


    4.1 The three types
    

    

    TypeHow it worksCharacterPhantom?Live use
    


    DynamicCoil on a diaphragm moves in a magnetic fieldRobust, handles huge SPL, slightly softer top endNoVocals, snare, guitar cabs, kick — anything loud or likely to get hit
    

    CondenserCharged diaphragm and backplate act as a capacitorDetailed, extended top end, more sensitiveYesOverheads, acoustic instruments, choirs, speech, anything needing detail
    

    RibbonThin metal ribbon suspended in a magnetic fieldSmooth, warm, naturally rolled-off topUsually not — can be damagingRare live. Brass, guitar cabs in studio-ish contexts. Fragile.
    

    

    Also worth knowing: large-diaphragm condensers (fuller, more flattering, more prone to handling noise) vs small-diaphragm or "pencil" condensers (more accurate, better off-axis behaviour, the standard for overheads and acoustic sources live).
    

    Watch it
    Ribbons are genuinely delicate. Don't blow into them, don't wave them around, don't send phantom to one unless the manufacturer explicitly says it's fine, and never plug one in with phantom already live. In a hire warehouse they should be in dedicated cases and handled as fragile stock.
    

    


    4.2 Polar patterns
    

    The pattern describes which directions a mic hears from. It's the most practically important spec on the box, because it determines both how much bleed you get and how much level you can get before feedback.
    

    

    PatternPicks upRejectsUse for
    


    CardioidFront, heart-shapedDirectly behindThe live default. Vocals, most close mic'ing.
    

    SupercardioidFront, narrowerSides strongly; small rear lobeLoud stages, tight rejection. Null is ~126° off axis.
    

    HypercardioidFront, narrowestSides very strongly; bigger rear lobeMaximum isolation. Null ~110°.
    

    OmniEverything, equallyNothingLavs, measurement mics, room mics. No proximity effect.
    

    Figure-8Front and backSides completelyM/S recording, two people facing each other, clever rejection tricks.
    

    ShotgunNarrow forward lobeSides (via interference tube)Distance pickup, broadcast, drama, corporate reinforcement of a stage.
    

    

    Standard
    The practical use of a polar pattern is aiming the null, not just the front. With a wedge on stage, you want the mic's dead spot pointing at the wedge. For a cardioid that's straight behind the mic — so wedges go directly in front of the singer. For a super/hypercardioid the null is off to the sides at the back, so wedges go in a pair at roughly 45°. Getting this right is worth more gain before feedback than any amount of EQ.
    

    


    4.3 Proximity effect & other physical realities
    

    

    Proximity effect
    All directional mics boost low frequencies as the source gets closer. A singer eating the mic gets a big warm boom; backing off two inches thins it out. Vocalists use this deliberately. You compensate with the high-pass filter.
    

    Off-axis colouration
    Sound arriving from the side isn't just quieter, it's differently coloured — usually duller. Good mics have smooth off-axis response; cheap ones sound honky when the singer turns their head.
    

    Plosives
    "P" and "B" sounds fire a blast of air at the diaphragm, producing a low thump. Fixed with a pop shield, a foam windshield, slight off-axis positioning, and a high-pass filter.
    

    Handling noise
    Vibration through the body of the mic. Worse on condensers and on mics without internal shockmounting. Shockmounts and stand isolation help.
    

    Wind
    Outdoors, a foam windshield is not enough. You need a proper furry ("dead cat", "windjammer"). Wind noise is huge, low-frequency, and eats your headroom.
    

    

    Standard
    Engage the high-pass filter on almost every channel that isn't kick, bass or a full-range source. Somewhere around 80–100 Hz on vocals, 100–120 Hz on most other things. It removes rumble, handling noise, stage vibration and plosive energy that contributes nothing but eats headroom. This is genuinely one of the highest-value habits in live sound.
    

    


    4.4 The stock — what you'll actually handle
    

    Vocal, handheld
    

    

    MicTypeNotes
    


    Shure SM58Dynamic cardioidThe industry default. Indestructible, forgiving, universally understood. If in doubt, this.
    

    Shure Beta 58ADynamic supercardioidBrighter, hotter, tighter pattern. More gain before feedback on a loud stage.
    

    Sennheiser e835 / e845Dynamic cardioid / superCommon alternative to the 58. Slightly more open sounding.
    

    Sennheiser e935 / e945Dynamic cardioid / superStep up. Many engineers prefer these to Betas.
    

    Shure Beta 87A / 87CCondenser super / cardioidDetailed handheld condenser. Great on good singers, unforgiving on loud stages.
    

    Neumann KMS 104 / 105CondenserPremium handheld. Beautiful, expensive, treat with care.
    

    Electro-Voice RE20 / RE50DynamicRE20 for broadcast/announce; RE50 is the classic omni reporter's handheld.
    

    

    Drums
    

    

    SourceUsual choices
    


    KickShure Beta 52A, AKG D112, Audix D6, Sennheiser e902, Shure Beta 91A (inside, boundary)
    

    SnareShure SM57 (the default), Beta 57A, Audix i5, Telefunken M80
    

    Hi-hatShure SM81, AKG C451, Rode NT5 — small-diaphragm condenser
    

    TomsSennheiser e604 / e904 (clip-on), Audix D2/D4, SM57
    

    OverheadsRode NT5, AKG C414, Neumann KM184, Shure SM81, Oktava MK-012
    

    

    Instruments & general
    

    

    SourceUsual choices
    


    Guitar cabSM57 (default), Sennheiser e906, Audix i5, Royer R-121 (ribbon, studio-ish)
    

    BassDI box, usually. Plus Beta 52A or D112 on the cab if wanted.
    

    Acoustic guitarDI from the pickup, and/or SM81/KM184/DPA 4099
    

    Brass / strings / woodwindDPA 4099 clip-on (the standard for live orchestral), SM57, e906
    

    PianoPair of condensers inside the lid, or DPA 4099P clip system
    

    Choir / ensembleHanging condensers, or SM81/KM184 on tall stands
    

    LecternGooseneck condenser, e.g. Shure MX418, Sennheiser MEG range
    

    Boundary / stage floorCrown PCC-160, Shure Beta 91A
