    Worn mics
    

    

    MicNotes
    


    DPA 4060 / 4061Premium omni lav. The theatre standard for a reason.
    

    DPA 4066 / 4088Headset — omni (4066) and directional (4088). Excellent, expensive, fragile.
    

    Countryman B3 / E6B3 lav, E6 earset. Robust, discreet, very common on corporate.
    

    Sennheiser MKE 1 / MKE 2Broadcast and theatre lavs.
    

    Shure MX150 / TwinPlexTwinPlex is Shure's premium range, increasingly common.
    

    

    Watch it
    Worn mics are the most expensive-per-gram and most abused items in the warehouse. Cables fail at the connector and at the capsule, sweat kills them, and they get yanked off. Check the termination matches the transmitter brand — a DPA with a Sennheiser 3.5 mm locking jack will not work on a Shure TA4F pack. Getting the wrong terminations on a job is a classic and totally avoidable prep failure.
    

    


    4.5 Placement crib sheet
    

    Starting points, not laws. Move the mic, listen, move it again — that's the entire skill.
    

    

    SourceStarting positionThen adjust for…
    


    Lead vocalGrille roughly at the lips, on axisProximity boom (back off), sibilance (slightly off axis)
    

    KickInside the port, 100–150 mm from the beater, aimed at the beaterMore click (closer to beater), more boom (further out / nearer the shell)
    

    Snare top25–50 mm above the rim, aimed at the centre, angled ~45°Hi-hat bleed (aim the null at the hat), body vs crack
    

    Snare bottomUnderneath aimed at the snares. Flip polarity.Wire rattle vs body
    

    Toms25–50 mm above the head, just inside the rim, angled inCymbal bleed, attack vs tone
    

    Hi-hat100–150 mm above the edge, aimed down, away from the snareSnare bleed, "chick" vs wash
    

    OverheadsEqual distance from the snare, ~1.2 m above the kitCymbal balance; measure with a cable to keep them equidistant
    

    Guitar cabOn the grille, aimed at the edge of the dust capCentre = bright and harsh; edge = warmer. Move a few cm at a time.
    

    Acoustic guitar150–200 mm out, aimed at the 12th fret — not the soundholeBoom (soundhole = too much), string noise
    

    Grand pianoPair over the strings, ~200 mm above, one over bass one over trebleLid position, bleed from the rest of the stage
    

    BrassSlightly off the bell axis, 150–300 mm outDirectly on axis is brutally bright and loud
    

    LecternGooseneck at ~200 mm from the mouth, aimed up at the facePresenters who lean away; consider two mics or a headset
    

    Panel / top tableOne mic per two people max, ideally one eachFeedback — see the 3:1 rule below
    

    

    Also seen
    There's a whole school of thought that says minimal mic'ing beats close mic'ing — two overheads and a kick mic on a jazz kit, a single pair on a string section. In small rooms and acoustic contexts this often sounds far better than 12 close mics. Don't assume more inputs is better.
    

    


    4.6 The 3:1 rule, and stereo techniques
    

    The 3:1 rule: when using multiple mics on one source or in one space, the distance between mics should be at least three times the distance from each mic to its source. This makes the bleed at least ~10 dB down, which keeps comb filtering from being audible. It's why panel discussions with a mic each sound fine and a badly-spaced pair of lectern mics sounds hollow.
    

    

    TechniqueSetupCharacter
    


    XYTwo cardioids, capsules coincident, 90°Perfectly mono-compatible, narrow image. Safe choice.
    

    ORTFTwo cardioids, 170 mm apart, 110°Natural, wide, good for ensembles and room capture.
    

    Spaced pair (A/B)Two omnis, 0.5–3 m apartBig and spacious; mono compatibility suffers.
    

    Mid/Side (M/S)Cardioid forward + figure-8 sideways, matrixedAdjustable width after the fact; perfect mono fold-down. Broadcast favourite.
    

    Decca treeThree omnis on a T frameOrchestral. Big rig, big sound, rarely your problem.
    

    

    


    4.7 Stands and accessories
    

    

    Tall boom
    The standard vocal/overhead stand. Heavy round base or tripod.
    

    Short boom
    Snare, toms, guitar cabs, kick. You need far more of these than people ever pack.
    

    Straight stand
    Simple, stable, no boom arm. Common for backing vocals and speech.
    

    Desk / table stand
    Top tables, panels, podium.
    

    Round base vs tripod
    Round base is more stable and tidier on stage (theatre and TV prefer them); tripod is lighter and cheaper, but the legs trip people and get in the way of a drum kit.
    

    Clip / clamp
    Every mic model has its own. They go missing constantly. Count them at prep.
    

    Shockmount
    Elastic cradle isolating the mic from stand vibration. For condensers.
    

    Pop shield
    Mesh or foam screen against plosives.
    

    Windshield / dead cat
    Foam for indoors, fur for outdoors.
    

    

    Watch it
    Two stand failures cause most on-stage incidents: a boom arm not tightened, which slowly droops through the show until the mic is at the singer's chest; and a tall boom with too much counterweight-free extension, which topples. Tighten every clutch properly, and set the base so the weight of the boom sits over a leg, not between them.
    

    


    4.8 Handling & care
    

      

    • Don't blow into a mic to test it. It's crude, it tells you almost nothing, and on a condenser or ribbon it can genuinely cause damage. Speak into it, or scratch the grille gently.
      • 

    • Don't tap the grille of a condenser either — it's a big impulse straight into a sensitive diaphragm.
      • 

    • Condensation kills condensers. Bringing a cold mic from a van into a warm room causes moisture on the diaphragm — you get crackling and low output. Let it acclimatise; don't panic and bin it.
      • 

    • Store in their cases/pouches, not loose in a drawer. Foam-lined mic cases exist for a reason.
      • 

    • Silica gel in mic cases is worth doing for expensive condensers and worn mics.
      • 

    • Clean grilles. Vocal mics get genuinely disgusting. Most unscrew — wash the grille and the foam in warm soapy water, dry completely before reassembling. This is a proper warehouse task and it matters for both sound and hygiene.
      • 

    • Handle by the body, not the grille. Grip oils and dents both cause problems.
      • 

    

    Standard
    Clean and check every vocal mic on return, not at the next prep. It's five minutes when it's part of the check-in routine and it's a crisis when you discover it at 8am with a van to load.
    

    


    


    

    PART 5
    Wireless & RF
    Its own discipline, its own vocabulary, and the thing most likely to make you look bad in front of an audience.
    

    


    5.1 Why RF gets its own part
    

    Everything else in this book is a chain you can trace with your hands. RF is invisible, shared with everyone else in the building and the surrounding area, legally regulated, and fails in ways that are hard to diagnose while a presenter is mid-sentence. It's also the area where a bit of knowledge makes you disproportionately valuable — a lot of technicians never get past "put a battery in it and hope".
    

    The good news: 90% of RF reliability comes from about six habits, and they're all in §5.9.
    

    


    5.2 Systems you'll meet
    

    

    FamilyTierNotes
    


    Shure BLX / SLX-DEntry / midSLX-D is digital, solid, very common in corporate hire stock.
    

    Shure QLX-DMidDigital, encryptable, good spectral efficiency. Workhorse.
    

    Shure ULX-DUpper midHigh channel density, excellent audio. Very widely hired.
    

    Shure Axient DigitalTopTouring/broadcast. Frequency diversity, remote control, interference detection.
    

    Sennheiser EW 100 G4 / EW-DEntry / midG4 is analogue and everywhere. EW-D is the digital replacement.
    

    Sennheiser EW-DXMid / upperCurrent digital workhorse range.
    

    Sennheiser 6000 / Digital 6000TopTheatre and broadcast standard.
    

    Sony DWXTopBroadcast favourite, very low latency.
    

    Audio-Technica 3000/5000Mid / upperGood value, less common in UK hire.
    

    

    Regardless of brand, a system is: a transmitter (handheld, bodypack, or plug-on), a receiver, and antennas. Everything else is refinement.
    

    

    Handheld
    Mic and transmitter in one. Capsules are often interchangeable — a Shure handheld body can take an SM58, Beta 58, KSM9 head. Check what capsule is fitted at prep; clients specify it.
    

    Bodypack
    Belt pack feeding a lav, headset, or instrument cable. Connector type is brand-specific and a classic prep trap.
    

    Plug-on
    Transmitter that clips onto the back of a normal XLR mic. Turns any wired mic wireless. Great for roving reporter mics and awkward positions; many supply phantom.
    

    

    


    5.3 Antennas
    

    

    TypePatternUse
    


    1/2-wave whipOmnidirectionalThe rubber aerial on the back of the receiver. Fine for short distances in the same room.
    

    Paddle / LPDADirectional, ~90°The flat triangular ones. More gain in one direction, rejects interference from behind. The standard upgrade.
    

    HelicalDirectional, circular polarisationLess sensitive to transmitter orientation. Good where performers move and tumble.
    

    Active antennaAnyHas an amplifier built in to overcome cable loss on long runs.
    

    

    Diversity
    

    Almost all professional receivers are true diversity: two antennas, two receiver sections, and the unit continuously picks whichever is getting the better signal. This defeats "dropouts" caused by multipath — the same signal arriving via two paths and cancelling itself at one point in space. Two antennas, spaced apart, are very unlikely to both be in a null at once.
    

    Standard
    Space diversity antennas roughly a wavelength apart (about 0.5 m at UHF) — or more — and angle them outwards at about 45° from each other. Get them above head height and with line of sight to the performers. Bodies are mostly water and water absorbs UHF; an antenna behind a crowd is an antenna in a swamp.
    

    Watch it
    Coax loses signal, and thin coax loses a lot. A long run of cheap RG-58 to a paddle can lose more than the paddle gains, making things worse. Use proper low-loss coax for long runs, keep runs as short as you can, and use an active antenna or in-line amplifier if you genuinely need distance.
    

    Antenna distribution
    

    Running more than about four receivers? Don't give each one its own pair of whips — they interfere with each other and it's a forest of aerials. Use an antenna distro: one pair of good antennas feeds a splitter which feeds all the receivers, and it usually passes DC to power active antennas and daisy-chains power to the receivers too. Cleaner, more reliable, less cable.
    

    


    5.4 UK spectrum — the legal bit
    

    Watch it
    Spectrum rules genuinely change — bands get sold off, boundaries shift, and what was legal five years ago may not be now. Check the current Ofcom PMSE position before you rely on anything in this section, and check the rules for the country you're in if you travel. Kit bought abroad may be illegal to transmit on here. Ofcom periodically runs a Sector Spectrum Review consultation covering PMSE alongside other spectrum users — these consultations are exactly the kind of thing that quietly reshapes which bands wireless mics and IEMs can legally use a few years out, so it's worth a search for the current one every so often rather than assuming today's bands are permanent.
    

    

    BandStatus in the UKPractical meaning
    


    Channel 38
    606.5–613.5 MHz    		Licensed — UK-wide shared accessCommon everyday hire-stock band. It is shared and non-protected, so a scan and a retune plan still matter.
    

    470–694 MHzLicensed, coordinated per site/date where availableUsed where channel count, venue and local spectrum conditions justify coordinated assignments. Do not assume a frequency is available just because a receiver tunes to it.
    

    Channel 70
    863–865 MHz    		Licence-exemptFree to use, no paperwork — but tiny (2 MHz), crowded, and shared with consumer gear. Fine for a couple of channels, hopeless for a show.
    

    821.5–832 MHz
    1785–1805 MHz    		Being made licence-exempt — Ofcom has decided this and expects to bring it in during 2026. Until Ofcom confirms it is in force, treat these as licensed.Useful extra options on compliant systems once exempt, but still not “set and forget”: check the exact equipment, interface requirements and local RF situation.
    

    2.4 GHzLicence-exemptShares with every WiFi network and Bluetooth device on the planet. Convenient, unpredictable in a crowd.
    

    

    Standard
    The realistic professional position: the company or RF lead owns the licence and coordination decision. For routine shared-band work, confirm which frequencies are authorised; for high channel counts or busy sites, use coordinated assignments. If hired equipment is supplied under someone else’s UK Wireless Microphone Licence, make sure the required written permit is in the job pack. If you're unsure, ask before the day — not on site.
    

    Current check
    UK PMSE spectrum has been actively changing. These bands were re-checked against Ofcom's published guidance in November 2026, when the exemption for 821.5–832 MHz and 1785–1805 MHz was still described as expected during 2026 rather than in force; always use the current Ofcom PMSE guidance for the exact job, equipment and date.
    

    Go deeper
    Ofcom's PMSE pages explain licence types and how to apply. If RF interests you, this is a specialism worth chasing — RF techs are in demand and it's a genuinely skilled niche. See §18.5.
    

    


    5.5 Coordination & intermodulation
    

    You can't just pick frequencies at random. Two transmitters don't only occupy their own frequencies — they mix together in the front end of receivers and produce intermodulation products at predictable mathematical relationships (the classic being 2×f1 − f2). Those products can land squarely on a third channel you're using, and that channel will be noisy or drop out even though nothing is obviously "on" its frequency.
    

    This is why manufacturers supply coordination groups — pre-calculated sets of frequencies that are intermod-clean with each other. Use them.
    

      

    1. Scan the spectrum on site to find what's already in use — TV transmissions, other companies' kit, the venue's own systems.
      2. 

    2. Coordinate — pick a clean group, either using the receiver's built-in group/channel scheme or software.
      3. 

    3. Deploy the frequencies to the transmitters, usually by IR sync from the receiver.
      4. 

    4. Document what's on what. Write it down. You will need it.
      5. 

    

    Standard
    Always scan on site, on the day, with the venue's own systems and the other departments' kit switched on. A scan done in an empty hall at 8am is a different spectrum from the one you'll have at 8pm. On multi-company events there is usually a designated RF coordinator — find them and get your frequencies from them rather than grabbing your own.
    

    Go deeper
    Shure Wireless Workbench and Sennheiser WSM are both free and both do proper coordination and monitoring. Learning one of them is a big, visible step up in capability. Links in §18.5.
    

    


    5.6 Batteries
    

    The most common cause of a wireless failure is a flat battery, and it's completely preventable.
    

      

    • Fresh batteries for every show, not every day, not "it looked fine". Standard
      • 

    • Good alkalines (Duracell Procell, Energizer Industrial) if you're on disposables. Cheap alkalines have wildly variable capacity and dump their voltage suddenly.
      • 

    • Never use zinc-carbon and be careful with generic rechargeable NiMH in analogue systems — their lower nominal voltage (1.2 V vs 1.5 V) means the receiver's battery meter reads wrong and you get much less warning.
      • 

    • Proper rechargeable systems (Shure SB900 series, Sennheiser BA series) report accurate remaining time in hours and minutes and are far better. If your company has them, use them and learn the charging discipline.
      • 

    • Battery contacts get corroded and bent. Clean them; check the pack door closes firmly. A pack that cuts out when the performer moves is often a mechanical contact problem, not RF.
      • 

    

    Standard
    Build a battery routine: new cells go in at a fixed point (e.g. at the top of soundcheck), used-but-good cells go in a separate labelled box for rehearsals and testing, and dead ones go straight in the recycling tub. Never let used and fresh mix in the same bag — that's how a "fresh" battery dies in Act Two.
    

    


    5.7 In-ear monitors (IEMs)
    

    Same RF principles, opposite direction: the transmitter is in the rack and the receiver is on the performer.
    

    

    Common systems
    Shure PSM 300 / PSM 900 / PSM 1000, Sennheiser EW IEM G4 and 2000 series, Lectrosonics.
    

    Mono vs stereo
    Most systems can run true stereo, or "MixMode" where one ear is the band and the other is vocals, blended with the pack's balance control.
    

    Combiner
    Multiple IEM transmitters into one antenna. Essential above two or three channels — otherwise the transmitters desensitise each other.
    

    Moulds vs universals
    Custom-moulded earpieces isolate far better and sound better. Generic tips are what you'll hire out. Hygiene matters — new tips per user.
    

    

    Watch it
    Keep IEM transmit antennas physically separated from mic receive antennas — different ends of the stage if you can, and at minimum a couple of metres apart. A transmitter next to a receiver's antenna will swamp its front end. This is the single most common cause of "the radio mics were fine until we added in-ears".
    

    Watch it
    IEMs sit directly in someone's ear canal. A feedback squeal, a dropped mic, or a mis-patch at full level can cause real hearing injury. Build the habit of bringing IEM levels up from zero, always limiting the IEM outputs, and never soloing something into a live IEM mix.
    

    


    5.8 Setting up and proving a wireless system
    

      

    1. Position antennas first — line of sight, above head height, away from metal, away from LED walls and lighting racks (both are RF-noisy).
      2. 

    2. Power up receivers only, all transmitters off, and scan. This shows you the noise floor and anything already occupying the band.
      3. 

    3. Assign frequencies from a clean coordinated group.
      4. 

    4. Sync each transmitter to its receiver (usually IR). Label the transmitter with the channel name — gaffa and a Sharpie, or proper channel tape.
      5. 

    5. Set transmitter gain so that the loudest expected input peaks near but not into the transmitter's limiter. This is set on the pack, and getting it wrong here cannot be fixed at the desk — too low is noisy, too high is distorted.
      6. 

    6. Check RF and AF meters on the receiver. Strong steady RF, healthy audio.
      7. 

    7. Walk test. Walk the entire performance area — stage, wings, backstage route, into the crowd if they go there — talking into the mic while someone watches the meters and listens. Find the dead spots before the show does.
      8. 

    8. Set squelch as low as reliably possible. Too high and you get dropouts on weak signal; too low and you get noise bursts when the transmitter is off.
      9. 

    9. Document the frequencies, the pack assignments and the gain settings.
      10. 

    

    Standard
    Do the walk test with the show conditions in place as far as possible — audience is the thing you can't replicate, so bias your margin generously. A system that's marginal in an empty room will fail in a full one.
    

    


    5.9 Diagnosing RF problems
    

    

    SymptomMost likely causeCheck
    


    Dropouts in one specific spotMultipath nullMove/re-angle antennas; check diversity is working
    

    Dropouts everywhere, worsening with distanceWeak signal — antenna placement or cable lossAntenna line of sight, coax length/quality, active antenna
    

    Sudden total lossBattery, or transmitter muted/switched offBattery, mute switch, pack door
    

    Noise bursts / hissSquelch too low, or interferenceRescan, raise squelch slightly, find the interferer
    

    Distorted audio, RF meter strongTransmitter gain too highTurn down gain on the pack
    

    Thin/noisy audio, RF strongTransmitter gain too lowTurn up gain on the pack
    

    Worked at 10am, fails at 7pmSpectrum changed — other users arrivedRescan and recoordinate
    

    Crackle when performer movesMic cable or connector at the packWiggle the capsule cable; swap the mic element
    

    Started when IEMs went inTransmit antenna too close to receive antennaSeparate them — see §5.7
    

    

    Standard
    Carry spares as a matter of course: a spare pack, a spare capsule, a spare lav, and a wired handheld with a long cable. The wired mic is the ultimate fallback — when RF has genuinely failed mid-show, a 20 m XLR and an SM58 saves the day and nobody in the audience knows anything happened.
    

    


    5.10 RF exposure & EMF safety
    

    Genuinely low on the list of things to worry about day to day, but worth actually knowing about rather than never hearing of it until someone asks you a question you can't answer. In the UK, the Control of Electromagnetic Fields at Work Regulations 2016 require employers to assess workplace exposure to electromagnetic fields — including RF — against exposure limits based on international (ICNIRP) guidance, and to control it where a real risk exists.
    

    Standard
    At the power levels and distances you'll actually work with — a handheld transmitter a performer is holding, a bodypack against their skin, a wedge-mounted receive antenna — this is not a realistic hazard. The situation actually worth knowing about is higher-power multi-channel IEM transmit combiners and antenna racks, where several transmitters' output is combined into one feed at meaningfully higher total power. Manufacturers of that class of kit publish a minimum safe working distance from the transmit antenna for exactly this reason — check the manual for anything you're not personally familiar with, and don't lean against or work for extended periods pressed right up against a live high-power transmit antenna.
    

    Also seen
    You are far more likely to be asked about this by a venue's own health and safety officer doing due diligence than to encounter an actual problem. Being able to say "our transmit power and distances are well within manufacturer guidance" is the correct answer, not a shrug.
    

    


    5.11 Shure and Sennheiser systems — step by step
    

    Most premium hire stock is Shure (Axient Digital, ULX-D, SLX-D) or Sennheiser (Digital 6000, EW-DX). The steps are the same shape on every system.
    

      

    1. Antennas on, receivers powered, outputs into the desk or stage box. With several receivers, use an antenna distribution system and remote paddles, not a forest of whips.
      2. 

    2. Turn on everything that will be on during the show — LED walls, video, other radio — then scan.
      3. 

    3. Coordinate. Shure: Wireless Workbench (free) — scan, add your devices' frequencies from the inventory, Analyze, Calculate, then Assign and Deploy to the networked receivers. Sennheiser: Wireless Systems Manager or Sennheiser Control Cockpit do the same job. On a single small system, the receiver's own group scan is fine.
      4. 

    4. Stay inside your licence — Channel 38, Channel 70, or the frequencies on your site licence (§5.12).
      5. 

    5. Batteries in (fresh AAs or the system's rechargeable packs, e.g. Shure SB900-series), transmitter on.
      6. 

    6. Sync each transmitter to its receiver channel (IR sync — hold the pack's window to the receiver's sync window).
      7. 

    7. Set transmitter gain/sensitivity so the loudest talker or singer doesn't clip, then label the pack and receiver channel with the person's name.
      8. 

    8. Walk test every mic (§11.6) and keep backups: spare mics already coordinated and synced.
      9. 

    

    Also seen
    Sennheiser Spectera and other new "wideband" (WMAS) systems carry many mics and IEMs in one wide channel. They're coordinated differently — follow the system owner's setup rather than the steps above.
    

    Sources · checked Nov 2026
    Shure Wireless Workbench quick start and ULX-D user guide (v6.8, 2026); Sennheiser product documentation. Menu names vary by model and firmware.
    

    


    5.12 UK licences in practice — what to buy and when
    

    

    RouteFrequenciesCost (Nov 2026)Use it for
    


    Licence-exemptUHF Channel 70: 863.1–864.9 MHz · VHF 173.7–175.1 MHz · 2.4 GHz below 10 mWFreeA handful of low-power mics; crowded, so expect to share
    

    UK Wireless Microphone Licence (shared)UHF Channel 38: 606.5–613.5 MHz (about 10–12 mics) · or 15 VHF spot frequencies£75 a year or £135 for two years bought on Ofcom's website (£85 / £155 otherwise)Everyday hire stock. Shared and unprotected — still scan
    

    Coordinated (standard) licenceOfcom assigns frequencies for a site and dateVaries with how many and how longBigger shows, more channels, protected frequencies. Apply well in advance
    

    

    Whoever owns the radio kit usually holds the licence — the hire company or the production. Your job is to know which licence the job is using and keep every transmitter (mics and IEMs) inside it. Using frequencies you aren't licensed for is a criminal offence under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006, and on mobile-network frequencies it interferes with phones.
    

    Watch it
    Cheap imported radio mics often transmit on frequencies that are illegal in the UK. If a client or band brings their own, check the frequency range before it goes on.
    

    Sources · checked Nov 2026
    Ofcom, PMSE licence information (fees and frequencies, checked Nov 2026); Ofcom PMSE sector review call for input (2026). Ofcom fees and bands change — check ofcom.org.uk before buying.
    

    


    


    

    PART 6
    PA & sound systems
    The output end: what the boxes are, how they go together and how a system serves a room safely.
    

    


    6.1 Anatomy of a loudspeaker
    

    

    Driver
    The moving part. A cone driver (woofer) for low and mid; a compression driver on a horn for high.
    

    Horn / waveguide
    The flare in front of the HF driver. It controls where the high frequencies go — the "dispersion pattern", quoted as e.g. 90° × 60° (horizontal × vertical).
    

    Crossover
    Splits the signal so each driver only gets the frequencies it can handle.
    

    Passive
    Crossover is inside the box, after the amplifier. One amp channel feeds the whole box. Simple, needs external amps.
    

    Active / powered
    Amplifier and DSP built into the box. Plug in mains and a signal. Dominant now for small and mid-scale work.
    

    Bi-amp / tri-amp
    Separate amp channels per driver, crossover done before the amps in DSP. More control, better performance, more cabling.
    

    

    Watch it
    A passive box wired to an amp with the wrong preset, or a bi-amp box fed a full-range signal on both inputs, will destroy the HF driver in seconds. Compression drivers handle a few watts; a woofer handles hundreds. If you're ever unsure whether a box is passive, active or bi-amp, find out before you send it signal.
    

    


    6.2 Types of box and what they're for
    

    

    TypeWhat it isUsed for
    


    Point sourceA single conventional boxSmall to mid rooms, fills, monitors. Simple and predictable.
    

    Line arrayMany small boxes hung in a vertical line, coupling togetherLong throw, large audiences, even coverage front to back
    

    Column arraySlim vertical column, often ground-standingReverberant rooms, speech, churches, discreet installs
    

    SubwooferLow frequencies only, typically below 80–120 HzWeight and impact. Almost always ground-stacked.
    

    Wedge / floor monitorAngled box pointing up at a performerStage monitoring
    

    SidefillLarger boxes at the sides of the stage facing acrossGeneral stage level
    

    Drum fillSub + top behind or beside the drummerDrummer's monitoring
    

    Front fillSmall boxes along the stage lipThe first few rows, who are under the main system's coverage
    

    Out fill / side fill (FOH)Additional hangs covering the edgesWide rooms the mains don't reach
    

    Delay stackSpeakers further back in the audience, time-delayedLong rooms/fields where the main system runs out of level
    

    

    


    6.3 Brands and ranges you'll handle
    

    

    TierTypical brands / ranges
    


    Portable activeRCF ART series, QSC K.2 / CP, Yamaha DXR / DZR, JBL EON, Electro-Voice ELX / ZLX, Turbosound iQ
    

    Mid-scale / small arraysRCF HDL, JBL VRX / SRX, Martin Audio Blackline X / Wavefront, Nexo ID / PS, EV EKX
    

    Pro touringd&b audiotechnik (E, xS, A, T, Y, V, CCL, KSL, XSL, GSL, plus the discontinued J and Q — every model in §6.20), L-Acoustics (X, A, Kara, K2/K3, K1, Syva), Meyer Sound (UPJ, LEO, LYON, PANTHER), Martin Audio MLA / Wavefront Precision, Adamson (S, E), Nexo STM/GEO
    

    Install / discreetBose, Tannoy, Community, K-array, d&b xS series
    

    

    Standard
    Learn your company's stock properly rather than trying to learn all of it. Know for each box: is it active or passive, what amp preset it needs, what it weighs, how it flies, what it draws, and what its dispersion is. That's the knowledge that makes you useful on site.
    

    Also seen
    Two more numbers on a loudspeaker's datasheet, alongside dispersion: sensitivity (the SPL it produces at 1 W of input, measured at 1 m — how efficiently it turns power into level) and maximum SPL (the loudest it can go before distortion or damage, at a stated distance). Neither is something you'll need to calculate as a junior, but recognise them for what they are when comparing two boxes or reading a spec sheet — a box with lower sensitivity just needs more amplifier power to reach the same level as one with higher sensitivity.
    

    


    6.4 Amplifiers & processing
    

    For passive systems, the amplifier is not a generic box — it's part of the loudspeaker system. Modern touring amps are really amplified DSP controllers: they contain the crossover, EQ, limiting and delay that make a specific box model behave correctly.
    

    

    d&b D20 / D40 / D80
    Amps for d&b systems. You must select the correct loudspeaker preset (d&b call it the setup) for the boxes connected. The whole d&b system — amps, output modes, setup and faults — is in §6.16–6.19.
    

    L-Acoustics LA4X / LA12X
    Same principle for L-Acoustics.
    

    Lab.gruppen, Powersoft, Camco, Crown, QSC
    General-purpose touring amplification, usually with configurable DSP.
    

    Outboard processor
    Where DSP isn't in the amp: BSS Soundweb / Blu, dbx DriveRack, Xilica, Symetrix. Sits between console and amps.
    

    

    Watch it
    The amp preset must match the box. Loading a preset for a different model — or worse, a "full range" preset onto a bi-amped enclosure — is the most expensive mistake in this part of the job. Check it every time, and check it again after anyone else has touched the rack. On a lot of systems this is a locked, password-protected setting for exactly this reason.
    

    


    6.5 Rigging & flying — the honest version
    

    Watch it
    Rigging is a qualified discipline and this section will not teach it to you. Flown loudspeakers weigh hundreds of kilos and hang over people. Do not attach, adjust, or sign off flown audio unless you are trained, competent and authorised to do so — and even then, under supervision until you're signed off. What follows is so you understand what's happening around you and can be a useful pair of hands, not so you can do it yourself.
    

    

    Ground stack
    Boxes stacked on the floor or on subs, often on a frame. Simpler, no rigging, but sightlines and coverage suffer.
    

    Flown
    Hung from the venue's structure via motors or fixed points. Better coverage, better sightlines, more skill and paperwork.
    

    Bumper / fly frame
    The top piece an array hangs from.
    

    Pull-back
    A second line pulling the bottom of an array backwards to set its angle.
    

    SWL / WLL
    Safe Working Load / Working Load Limit — the rated maximum. Never exceeded, never guessed.
    

    Secondary / safety
    A backup attachment that catches the load if the primary fails.
    

    LOLER / PUWER
    The UK regulations covering lifting equipment and its inspection. See §13.3.
    

    

    Standard
    Universal rule on any site: nobody stands under a suspended load. Not "briefly", not "just to plug this in". If a motor is moving, the area below it is clear. Learn to notice this and step out of the way without being told — people notice.
    

    


    6.6 Coverage, aiming and subs
    

    The job of system design is getting roughly the same experience everywhere in the audience. That means aiming boxes at people, not at walls, and accepting that the front will always be louder than the back.
    

    Point source aiming
    

    Aim the box so its on-axis line points at the furthest listeners, not the nearest. The near listeners are already close (loads of level from proximity) and are covered by the off-axis spill. Aiming at the front row wastes your throw and deafens them.
    

    Sub configurations
    

    

    ArrangementWhat it does
    


    Left/right stacksSimple, but creates a "power alley" of coupling down the centre and cancellation at the sides.
    

    Centre cluster / mono subsAll subs together in the middle. Even coverage, no power alley. Very common now.
    

    Cardioid subsOne or more subs reversed and processed so the energy behind the stack cancels. Keeps bass off the stage and out of the neighbours' windows.
    

    End-fireSubs in a line front-to-back, each delayed, so energy adds forwards and cancels backwards. Needs depth but works beautifully.
    

    Sub arc / gradientCurved or delay-shaded lines to widen or shape the low-frequency coverage.
    

    

    Standard
    Cardioid or end-fire subs are worth understanding early, because they solve two problems at once: they clean up the stage (happier musicians, less low-end mud in the mics) and they cut the noise complaint risk from behind the stage. On a lot of jobs they're the difference between passing and failing the noise conditions.
    

    Also seen
    At the top end of touring and festival work you'll increasingly meet immersive or object-based audio — systems like L-Acoustics L-ISA or d&b Soundscape, which use many individually-controlled boxes across the width of a room (rather than one stereo pair) to place sounds precisely and move them around the space, plus ambisonic approaches for fully surrounding a room. It's a specialism of its own, well beyond what this book covers — worth knowing it exists so a job spec mentioning it doesn't come as a surprise, not something you're expected to already understand.
    

    


    6.7 Prediction software
    

    Before a system is built, it's modelled. Every major manufacturer supplies free software that predicts coverage and SPL for their own boxes in a given room.
    

    

    d&b ArrayCalc
    For d&b systems. Pairs with R1 for control.
    

    L-Acoustics Soundvision
    For L-Acoustics. Pairs with LA Network Manager.
    

    Meyer MAPP
    Meyer's prediction tool.
    

    Martin Audio DISPLAY
    For Martin systems, especially MLA.
    

    Nexo NS-1
    Nexo's version.
    

    EASE / EASE Focus
    Cross-manufacturer. EASE Focus is free and covers many brands — a great one to learn on.
    

    

    Go deeper
    Download EASE Focus and model a room you know — your local venue, your workplace. Being able to say "that hang will hit the back wall hard, we should steer it down" with a picture to back it up is a genuinely senior skill and you can start learning it tonight for free.
    

    


    6.8 System tuning — what's actually happening
    

    You won't be tuning systems yet, but knowing what the systems tech is doing means you can help rather than hover.
    

      

    1. Verification — prove every box works, is on the right preset, and is polarity-correct. Boring, essential, and often the bit you'll be doing.
      2. 

    2. Level matching — get all the subsystems (mains, fills, delays) to comparable levels.
      3. 

    3. Time alignment — delay the nearer subsystem so its sound arrives at the same moment as the further one. A delay stack 30 m back needs roughly 87 ms of delay (sound travels about 344 m/s, so ~2.9 ms per metre).
      4. 

    4. Crossover alignment — get the subs and tops working together at the crossover point rather than cancelling.
      5. 

    5. EQ — correct broad tonal problems in the system's response. Not fixing the room; you cannot EQ a room (§6.15).
      6. 

    6. Listen — with known reference material, from several places in the room. Measurement gets you to sensible; ears get you to good.
      7. 

    

    Also seen
    There's a real philosophical split here. One camp measures extensively with Smaart or similar and tunes to a target curve. Another camp tunes almost entirely by ear with familiar tracks. Most good engineers do both — measure to find and fix real problems, then listen to make it sound right. Be suspicious of anyone who says one method is the only method.
    

    Go deeper
    This is the deepest rabbit hole in live audio and it's genuinely fascinating. Rational Acoustics (Smaart) run training; the Bob McCarthy book Sound Systems: Design and Optimization is the standard text. See §18.6 and §18.7.
    

    


    6.9 Monitor world
    

    Stage monitoring is a separate craft from FOH and arguably harder — you're building six to sixteen different mixes simultaneously for people who can't tell you what's wrong except by pointing.
    

    

    Wedges
    Angled floor boxes. Aimed at the performer's head, positioned so the vocal mic's null faces them.
    

    Mix count
    How many independent monitor mixes you're providing. Every performer wanting their own is expensive in outputs and time.
    

    Pre-fade sends
    Monitor sends are pre-fade so FOH fader moves don't change what the band hears. This is close to universal and getting it wrong is very obvious.
    

    Ringing out
    Deliberately pushing a monitor until it feeds back, identifying the frequency, and cutting it — repeated a few times to raise gain before feedback.
    

    Graphic EQ
    Traditionally a 31-band GEQ per wedge. Still the standard on many desks.
    

    

    Also seen
    Ringing out a wedge with a graphic before soundcheck is the traditional approach and still widely done. Others prefer to leave the monitor flat and only cut narrow parametric notches reactively when something actually rings, arguing that pre-emptive ringing out just makes everything sound worse for a problem that might not occur. Both are legitimate; the second is increasingly common with modern boxes and good mic technique.
    

    Watch it
    Never point a wedge at the back of a vocal mic, never let someone stand between the wedge and their own mic, and never turn a monitor up "just to check" while someone's face is next to it. Feedback at wedge level is painful and can damage hearing.
    

    


    6.10 Loudness, limits and the law
    

    

    dBA
    A-weighted — approximates human sensitivity, discounts bass heavily. What most noise conditions are written in.
    

    dBC
    C-weighted — much flatter, includes the low end. Better for measuring what actually annoys neighbours.
    

    Leq
    Equivalent continuous level — an average over a period, e.g. "Leq 15 min". This is how limits are usually written, not as an instantaneous peak.
    

    Venue noise limiter
    A device that cuts the power to the stage if the level exceeds a threshold. Common in function rooms and hotels. Find out if there is one, where it is and what it's set to before you build.
    

    Licence conditions
    Many events have legally binding noise limits and curfews as conditions of the premises licence (or, for smaller one-off events, a Temporary Event Notice) granted under the Licensing Act 2003. For bigger or higher-risk events, a Safety Advisory Group — the local authority, police, fire and other agencies working together — reviews the event and can set or tighten these conditions, often drawing on the guidance in the Purple Guide. That matters practically: a limit breach isn't just "the neighbours are annoyed", it's a breach of a legal condition the promoter's licence depends on, which is why the SAG or an environmental health officer can shut a show down over it. Breaching them has consequences for the promoter, not just embarrassment.
    

    

    Watch it
    Protect your hearing from day one. Hearing damage is cumulative, permanent and completely invisible until it's done. The UK Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 set action levels at 80 dB(A) and 85 dB(A) daily exposure — a loud gig blows past both. Carry decent filtered earplugs (Alpine, Etymotic, EarPeace — around £20 and they don't muffle) and get custom moulds when you can afford them (£150–200, last years). Every experienced engineer you meet either wears them or wishes they had.
    

    


    6.11 Assistive listening & hearing loops
    

    Not part of the PA, but genuinely part of the job — audio techs are very often the ones who end up responsible for these, simply because they're the closest thing to "audio" on site.
    

    

    What it is
    A hearing/induction loop is a wire run around a room (or a smaller area, sometimes called a counter loop) driven by a dedicated loop driver amplifier. It creates a magnetic field carrying the audio, which a hearing aid's built-in T-coil picks up directly — bypassing the room's background noise entirely, rather than just amplifying it along with everything else.
    

    The legal side
    Under the Equality Act 2010, venues are expected to make reasonable adjustments for disabled customers, which in practice includes providing a working induction loop. Building Regulations Part M requires hearing enhancement systems in new or altered buildings at reception points, performance areas and meeting spaces — marked with the standard blue "ear and T" symbol.
    

    Feeding it
    The loop driver wants a dedicated mono line-level feed of the primary programme audio — usually a matrix or aux send from the console — not a stray mic picking up the room. A room mic gives loop users the room's echo and noise along with the speech; a proper feed gives them exactly what everyone else is hearing, cleanly.
    

    The standard
    IEC 60118-4 sets the technical requirements — field strength, frequency response and signal-to-noise ratio — that a compliant loop has to meet. You're not expected to certify a system yourself, but knowing the standard exists is enough to recognise when a "we've got a loop" claim needs an actual test, not just a knowing nod.
    

    

    Standard
    If a venue tells you they have an induction loop, ask when it was last tested and who feeds it — a genuinely surprising number of installed loops are silently unplugged, mis-patched, or fed from the wrong source. If you're asked to feed one yourself, a dedicated send from the console, checked with a level that's neither buried nor distorted, is the whole job.
    

    Go deeper
    Ampetronic and Contacta both publish clear, freely available technical guides on loop systems aimed at installers rather than end users — genuinely useful if you end up dealing with these regularly. See §18.11.
    

    


    6.12 Interpretation & conference systems
    

    The conference-world cousin of the hearing loop — and the same pattern applies: audio techs very often end up owning it, again simply because it's the closest thing to "audio" on site, even though it's really its own small discipline.
    

    

    What it is
    Simultaneous interpretation lets a speaker be heard live in another language — an interpreter in a soundproofed booth listens on headphones and speaks the translation into a mic, which is transmitted to delegates on wireless IR or RF receivers with earpieces, channel-selectable if there's more than one target language.
    

    Your part in it
    Almost always just the feed — the interpreters need a clean, dedicated feed of the source language audio (the same discipline as a broadcast submix, §14.8), and their translated output needs to be received back into the system correctly if it's being mixed into a recording or a specific zone. You are not expected to manage the booths or receivers themselves — that's normally a specialist interpretation-equipment supplier's job.
    

    What to check
    Which channel is which language, that the interpreter feed is live and clean before delegates arrive, and — if it's your job to supply it — that the receiver count matches the expected audience, with spares. A silent interpretation channel five minutes into a conference is a much bigger problem than a silent audio channel, because there's no way for that portion of the audience to follow anything until it's fixed.
    

    

    Standard
    Treat the interpreter feed with the same care as a broadcast feed — test it properly before doors with the interpreters actually present, not just by yourself. They'll tell you immediately if the level or source is wrong, and they're the only people in the building who can.
    

    


    6.13 Audio description
    

    The theatre-world accessibility service that's easy to miss entirely if nobody's ever pointed it out to you — a describer narrates the visual action (movement, expressions, set changes) into the gaps between dialogue, for blind and partially-sighted audience members listening on a headset. In the UK, specialist providers like VocalEyes train describers and often run the service itself; the venue's job, and by extension yours, is mostly making sure the infrastructure works.
    

    

    What you're actually asked for
    A clean feed of the show mix to the describer's booth or position (so they can hear what the audience hears while they narrate), and a transmission system — usually the same IR or RF infrastructure as an interpretation system (§6.12) — carrying the describer's voice out to headset receivers in the audience.
    

    Touch tours
    Many venues offer a pre-show "touch tour" letting blind patrons handle set pieces, props and sometimes costumes to build a mental picture before the performance. Not really an audio job, but you'll sometimes be asked to support it with a portable PA or just a quiet, working comms channel.
    

    What to check
    Same discipline as the interpreter feed — test it live, with the describer present, before doors. A describer who can't hear the show clearly can't do their job at all.
    

    

    Standard
    Tickable version of all of the above, covering audio description alongside interpretation and hearing loops together, at §19.15, the access services checklist.
    

    


    6.14 Outdoor & weather-exposed work
    

    Everything above assumes a roof. A genuinely large share of UK live audio doesn't have one — festivals, outdoor corporate, marquees with open sides — and weather causes its own specific category of problems worth knowing before you meet them for the first time.
    

    

    IP ratings
    The two-digit code on outdoor-rated boxes (IP54, IP55, IP65…) — first digit is protection against solid objects/dust, second is against water. IP54 (dust-protected, splash-resistant) is a common minimum for touring outdoor boxes; IP55 adds stronger jet protection; IP65 (fully dust-tight, low-pressure jet resistant) is typical for permanent outdoor install. A box with no IP rating at all almost certainly isn't meant to get rained on, whatever it looks like.
    

    Electronics in the wet
    Consoles, racks and anything with an unsealed connector are the actual risk, not the speakers — rain covers (fitted covers, gazebos, or simply a tarp rigged with a run-off slope so water doesn't pool) over FOH and any exposed patch bays are standard on any outdoor job, wired or not.
    

    Wind
    Rumbles and thumps on open mics, especially outdoor vocal or speech mics — a foam windshield helps a little, a proper wind muff ("dead cat") helps a lot more. Wind also physically moves line array elements and lightweight boxes on stands, which is a rigging and PUWER concern (§13.3) as much as an audio one.
    

    Temperature
    Cold weather drains batteries faster and makes wireless receivers slightly less predictable at the margins of range — carry more spares than you think you need on a cold outdoor day. Direct sun on a black console or amp rack for hours can push internal temperatures high enough to matter; shade it if you can.
    

    

    Watch it
    Never work on live electrical connections in the rain, and if lightning is genuinely close, that's a stop-the-show safety call for the Event Safety Officer or Production Manager, not something to quietly push through. Outdoor events should have a written severe weather plan — ask to see it if one job feels like it might need it.
    

    Standard
    Tickable version of all of the above at §19.14, the outdoor & weather-exposed job checklist.
    

    


    6.15 The room is part of the system
    

    Everything up to here has been about the boxes. But the audience never hears the boxes on their own — they hear the boxes plus the room, and in a difficult building the room is the louder partner. This is the bit that explains why the same PA can sound superb in one venue and like a swimming pool in the next, and why §6.8 insists you can't EQ a room.
    

    

    Direct sound
    What arrives straight from the loudspeaker, first. It carries the intelligibility — the consonants that let someone understand a word rather than just hear a noise.
    

    Reflections
    The same sound arriving later, having bounced off a wall, the ceiling or the floor. Early reflections (within roughly 30 ms) mostly reinforce the direct sound. Later ones smear it.
    

    Reverberation
    What's left once the reflections are too many and too close together to hear individually — a decaying wash. Measured as reverberation time (RT60): how long it takes to decay by 60 dB after the source stops.
    

    Room modes / standing waves
    At low frequencies, wavelengths are comparable to the room's dimensions, so the room resonates at particular frequencies. That's why bass can be overwhelming in one seat and almost missing three metres away, with nothing wrong with the system.
    

    Absorption
    Soft things — curtains, carpet, seating, and above all people — turn sound energy into a tiny amount of heat instead of reflecting it. This is why a room measured empty is not the room you'll be mixing in.
    

    

    Rough expectations, so you know what you're walking into: a well-treated studio or a small meeting room might be a few tenths of a second of RT60; a decent theatre around a second; a big church, atrium or sports hall three seconds or more. Above roughly two seconds, speech intelligibility is genuinely hard to achieve and the system design has to fight for it.
    

    Standard
    You can't remove reverberation, so you avoid feeding it. That means directivity — using boxes whose pattern puts energy on people and not on walls and ceilings (§6.6), getting sources closer to listeners with fills or delays rather than turning the mains up, and choosing column arrays or tight-pattern boxes in reverberant rooms (§6.2). Turning it up in a live room makes the reverberation louder too, so it makes things worse, not better.
    

    Watch it
    An empty room and a full room are different acoustic spaces. A few hundred people are a large amount of absorption, mostly in the mid and high frequencies — so the room gets drier and slightly duller once doors open. A system tuned to sound perfect in an empty hall at 3pm will usually want a little more top end at 8pm. Don't panic-EQ during the first song; expect the change and leave yourself somewhere to go.
    

    Also seen
    You'll hear people talk about the critical distance — the point where the reverberant field is as loud as the direct sound. Closer than that and intelligibility is mostly fine; further away and it drops off fast however loud you go. It's a useful mental model for why a delay speaker halfway back fixes a problem that another 3 dB at the front never will.
    

    Watch it
    Acoustic treatment is not your call to make. Hanging drapes, moving absorbers or altering a listed building's surfaces belongs to the venue and the production designer. What you can reasonably do is point out that a hard, reflective room will limit what the system can achieve, early enough for someone to decide about drapes — and that conversation lands far better at the advance stage (§1.7) than at soundcheck.
    

    Go deeper
    Room acoustics is a full discipline and this is deliberately only the working tech's share of it. If it grabs you, it's the natural companion to system tuning (§6.8) — the Bob McCarthy book in §18.7 covers the interaction between systems and rooms properly, and modelling a familiar room in EASE Focus (§6.7) makes the effect visible rather than theoretical.
    

    


    6.16 d&b audiotechnik — how the system fits together
    

    d&b is one of the brands you're most likely to meet on UK touring, theatre and corporate work, and it works differently from a rack of generic amps and passive boxes. The thing to understand first: d&b sell a system, not separate parts. Almost every d&b loudspeaker is passive, and is designed to be driven only by a d&b amplifier running the matching loudspeaker setup for that exact box. The setup holds the crossover, EQ and — most importantly — the protection that keeps that model's drivers alive.
    

    

    Loudspeaker
    The box. Passive, with NL4 input and link sockets (some older or install models differ). Its model name is the setup you'll need.
    

    Amplifier
    A d&b amp, four channels on current models, with DSP inside. Each channel is told which box it's driving.
    

    Setup
    The loudspeaker preset — d&b's word for it. Chosen per channel. Wrong setup, wrong sound at best, damaged drivers at worst.
    

    Cable
    NL4 (or NL8 multicore). Part of the system — the amp can even correct for its length (LoadMatch, below).
    

    Software
    ArrayCalc to design it, R1 to control and monitor it.
    

    

    The amplifiers you'll meet
    

    

    AmpWhat to know
    


    D6 / D12Older two-channel amps, still in plenty of hire stock. Small LCD and buttons; remote control over CAN bus rather than Ethernet. Pinouts differ slightly from the current amps — read the label above the outputs.
    

    D20Four-channel, 2U, touchscreen. Now discontinued but still the everyday workhorse in a lot of stock, for E, Y, V, T, A and xS boxes. Four analogue (XLR) and two AES digital inputs, four individual NL4 outputs, two centre NL4s for paired modes, and an NL8. Not for J-Series, M2 or SL-Series.
    

    D80Four-channel high-power touring amp — runs the larger systems the D20 can't. Same touchscreen logic, outputs as NL4 (or EP5 on some versions) plus NL8.
    

    D25The newest (2025): a four-channel amp for smaller, high-efficiency mobile systems, with Milan networking like the D40/D90.
    

    D40 / D90The newer generation. Milan (AVB) networking built in alongside analogue and AES, plus a built-in web interface as well as R1 control. The D90 drives the highest-power systems.
    

    5D / 10D / 30D / 40DInstallation amps. You'll find them in venues rather than in hire stock — usually somebody else's system, so look but don't change.
    

    

    The loudspeaker ranges
    

    

    RangeTypical use
    


    E-Series (E6, E8, E12…), Q-SeriesOlder but very common: small point source, fills, delays, corporate. Q is a compact line/point system still in many stocks.
    

    xS-Series (5S, 8S, 10S…), A-SeriesCurrent point source and augmented arrays — fills, small rooms, theatre, corporate.
    

    T-SeriesCompact box that switches between line-array and point-source use. Small arrays, theatres, corporate.
    

    Y-Series, V-SeriesMid-to-large line arrays with matching point-source boxes and subs. Touring and festivals.
    

    CL-Series (CCL)Compact cardioid line array (2025) on a single amp channel per box. Small to mid-size venues and tours.
    

    J-Series, SL-Series (KSL, GSL, XSL)Large-format touring arrays. SL boxes are cardioid by design — they control their own low end behind the array.
    

    M-Series (M4, M2…)Stage monitors / wedges.
    

    …-SUB and B-SeriesSubwoofers. Several are designed to be run in cardioid arrangements (§6.6).
    

    

    Every model, and which amp drives it — §6.20 → Amps, loudspeakers, the naming, and what's discontinued.
    

    The software around it
    

    

    ArrayCalc
    d&b's free design software (§6.7). The system tech models the room and the boxes, and ArrayCalc works out angles, rigging loads, delays — and which amp channel drives which box with which setup. It exports a project for R1.
    

    ArrayProcessing
    An ArrayCalc option that calculates individual filters for every box in a line array to shape its coverage and tonal balance front to back. Applied through the amps; never "tweak it" by hand.
    

    R1 Remote control
    The laptop software that shows and controls every amp on the network: setups, levels, mutes, delays, EQ, and live meters. Current amps connect over Ethernet (OCA / AES70); D6/D12-era amps need a CAN interface.
    

    LoadMatch
    On current amps, compensates electrically for the speaker cable — so a box at the end of a long run sounds like one on a short run (d&b quote up to 70 m). It needs the real cable length and cross-section entered, so note them as you run cable.
    

    System check
    On current amps, measures each connected loudspeaker against a reference taken when the system was known to be good, and flags a missing box, a dead driver or a bad cable. Most useful when the reference was taken at prep.
    

    

    Standard
    Every d&b job has a plan: an ArrayCalc file, an R1 project, or at minimum a patch sheet from the system tech — box, amp, channel, mode, setup. Work from it, and if you're handed a d&b system with no plan, ask for one before you configure anything.
    

    Watch it
    Never drive a d&b box from a generic amp, or from a d&b amp in "linear" mode, unless the system owner has specifically said to. Without its setup the box has no protection at all — the HF driver is the first thing to go.
    

    Go deeper
    d&b publish free video tutorials for each amp (overview, input modes, output modes, channel setup), and run in-person workshops — in the UK at Nailsworth — including d&basics (loudspeakers, amps and choosing the right system) and Software & System Fundamentals (ArrayCalc and R1, from data entry to simulation and output). Dates, places and costs are on d&b's workshops page. ArrayCalc and R1 are both free downloads, and R1 can open a project offline, so you can learn the screens on your own laptop before you're ever near a live rack.
    

    


    6.17 d&b amps — output modes, connectors and the front panel
    

    The single most important thing on a d&b amp is the output mode, because it decides which socket a speaker cable goes into and which pins carry what. Get the mode and the socket to agree and almost everything else follows. The table below is how the current four-channel amps (D20, D80 and their successors) work: channels pair up as A/B and C/D, and each pair has its own mode.
    

    

    Output modeUsed forPlug intoNL4 pins
    


    Dual ChannelPassive full-range boxes and subs, one channel each. Each channel's setup chosen independently (top or sub).The individual outputs A, B, C, D1± and 2± both carry that one channel (wired in parallel) — any box will work on any 2- or 4-core cable
    

    Mix TOP/SUBA passive top and a sub on one cable. Channel A (C) runs the top setup, channel B (D) the sub setup.The centre A/B (or C/D) output1± = top (A or C) · 2± = sub (B or D). Needs a 4-core cable
    

    2-Way Actived&b boxes driven actively — a separate amp channel for low and high frequencies.The centre A/B (or C/D) output1± = LF (A or C) · 2± = MF/HF (B or D). Needs a 4-core cable
    

    NL8 outputFour channels down one 8-core multicoreThe NL81± = A · 2± = B · 3± = C · 4± = D
    

    

    That's why d&b boxes are built the way they are: on d&b's usual convention a top listens on pins 1 and a sub listens on pins 2, and the link socket on each box passes all four poles through. So a single 4-core cable from the centre A/B output can go to a sub and link on to a top, and each hears only its own channel. Every d&b cabinet has its pin use printed beside its connectors — read it when you're unsure.
    

    Watch it
    Older amps (D6, D12) and EP5-fitted amps don't follow exactly this layout. Always read the label above the outputs — it states the mode and pins for each socket — and check the amp's manual if anything doesn't match the table.
    

    Inputs
    

    

    Analogue
    XLR inputs (A1–A4 on a D20), with XLR link outputs to feed the next amp.
    

    Digital (AES3)
    XLR inputs carrying two channels each (D1/2, D3/4), with a digital link out. The amp must lock to the sample rate (48 or 96 kHz).
    

    Network
    D40/D90: Milan (AVB) built in. D20/D80: Dante arrives through a bridge (such as d&b's DS10) converting to AES.
    

    Input mode / routing
    Each amp has an input mode (analogue, digital, network), and each channel is routed from one or more inputs. Current amps can also fall back to a second input if the first one is lost — handy, and also a reason a channel can be playing from somewhere unexpected.
    

    

    Reading the front panel
    

    

    IndicatorMeansWhat to do
    


    Green — ISP / OSPInput Signal Present (and, on touchscreen amps, Output Signal Present in brighter green). Signal is reaching the channel.No green with the source playing → the problem is upstream of the amp, or in its input routing.
    

    Yellow — GRGain Reduction: the channel's limiter is working (more than about 3 dB). Not a fault — the box has reached its limits.Ease off at the console. If it lights at modest level, check the setup is right for the box.
    

    Red — OVL / muteOn D6/D12, overload: input too hot or heavy limiting. On the touchscreen amps the channel strip also shows red when a channel is muted. The screen says which.Reduce the input level, or find out who muted it and why before you unmute.
    

    Error / warning textOver-temperature, mains, output or hardware faults, reported on the screen and in R1.Write the exact text down, tell the system owner. Don't keep power-cycling it.
    

    

    The channel settings you'll see
    

    On each channel: setup (the box), level, delay, mute, user EQ, and a handful of switchable functions that depend on the box — for example CUT (a high-pass that takes the low end out of a top when it's running with subs), HFA (gentle high-frequency roll-off for nearby listeners), CPL (compensates for boxes coupling together at low frequencies) and cardioid or INFRA options on some subs. Which ones are switched on is a design decision: copy them from the plan, don't improvise.
    

    Standard
    Current d&b amps have a built-in pink-noise and sine generator per channel. Combined with mutes it's the quickest way to prove one box at a time without needing anyone at the console — but agree it with the system tech first, and start with the level down.
    

    


    6.18 Setting up a d&b system, start to finish
    

    The sequence for a typical ground-stacked or simple flown d&b system, as the person doing the physical work and the first checks. On a big system a system tech drives the software — this is so you can do your part properly and know what comes next. Rigging stays with the people qualified for it (§6.5).
    

      

    1. Get the plan. ArrayCalc file, R1 project or patch sheet: which box, which amp and channel, which output mode, which setup, which functions (CUT etc.), delays and levels. No plan, ask.
      2. 

    2. Prep it in the warehouse. Count boxes, amps, speaker cables (4-core where the plan uses Mix TOP/SUB or 2-Way Active), NL8 multicores and breakouts, plus spares. Test every speaker cable (§3.12). Power each amp up, check it boots without errors and has the setups needed. If the amps support System check, this is the moment to take a known-good reference.
      3. 

    3. Position amps close to the boxes they drive — short speaker runs are better than long ones. Mains in through powerCON from the agreed distro, locked. Leave racks room to breathe front and back.
      4. 

    4. Run the speaker cables. Right connector for the mode (individual outputs for Dual Channel, centre A/B or C/D for paired modes). Lock every speakON at both ends, label both ends with amp and channel, and note the length if LoadMatch is in use.
      5. 

    5. Run signal to the amps — analogue, AES or network — and feed the link outputs on to the next amp as the plan says.
      6. 

    6. Power up in order: console and processing first, amps last — with amp channels muted. (Power down in reverse: amps first.)
      7. 

    7. Configure each amp, either by loading the R1 project or at the front panel: input mode and routing, output mode per channel pair, setup per channel, functions, level, delay, EQ, LoadMatch cable data. Check each channel against the plan. Lock the front panels if that's the house rule.
      8. 

    8. Connect R1. Laptop on the control network; every amp has a unique Remote ID / address; match the devices to the project and go online. Every amp should appear with no warnings.
      9. 

    9. Run System check if the amps support it, and look into anything it flags before going further.
      10. 

    10. Prove it box by box. Low-level pink noise or a known track to one channel at a time; everything else muted. Walk to each box: right box answering, every driver working, nothing rattling, sub and top on the right channels. Then check polarity with the system tech's method.
      11. 

    11. Then the whole system — level balance between sections, sub-to-top alignment, delays, tuning (§6.8). This is the system tech's call; your job is to be useful and keep the area clear.
      12. 

    12. Save and write it down. Save the R1 project with the date, and note anything that changed from the plan and why. That note is what makes the derig and the next job easy.
      13. 

    

    Watch it
    Two things to never skip, however short the turnaround: check the setup on every channel against the box it's actually driving (it's the most expensive mistake on a d&b rig), and mute before you plug or unplug any speaker cable.
    

    Standard
    Derig is the same list backwards: mute, power amps down, unplug and coil speaker cables (checking each for damage as you go), then signal and mains. Anything that misbehaved on the job gets labelled and reported, not packed (§11.5).
    

    


    6.19 d&b & speakON fault-finding
    

    Start with the general method (§12.1) and the first sixty seconds (§12.8), then use this table. Work left to right through the checks, one change at a time, and read the amp's channel indicators first — they tell you which half of the system the fault is in.
    

    

    SymptomCheck, in order
    


    One box silent, its amp channel shows green (signal present)Channel muted? → speakON locked at both ends? → cable on the right output for the mode? → 4-core if the box needs pins 2? → swap in a known-good cable → try the box on a known-good channel. If the fault follows the box, quarantine it.
    

    Channel shows no input signalSource actually playing and unmuted at the console? → amp input mode (analogue vs digital vs network) → that channel's input routing → the signal cable or AES link → digital lock / sample rate → Dante bridge or Milan stream.
    

    Sub silent, tops fine (Mix TOP/SUB)Cable only 2-core, or an NL2 somewhere in the run → cable in an individual output instead of the centre A/B → channel B (D) not running a sub setup, or muted.
    

    Top silent, sub fineChannel A (C) muted or wrong setup → link cable between sub and top faulty or not locked → top plugged into a socket the mode doesn't feed.
    

    Box sounds dull / no top end2-Way Active run with a cable missing pins 2 → HFA switched on where the plan doesn't want it → wrong setup → damaged HF driver (listen close at low level; quarantine if confirmed).
    

    Thin / no bass from a top that should have itCUT switched on with no subs running → wrong setup.
    

    Yellow GR on constantlyNot a fault: the box is at its limit. Turn down at the console. If it happens at modest level, check the setup matches the box and that the input isn't hugely over-driven.
    

    Red on a channelRead the screen: muted (find out who and why) or overloaded (reduce the level feeding the amp).
    

    Crackle, cutting out, worse when the cable movesspeakON a quarter-turn short of locked → worn connector → damaged cable. Swap the cable to isolate it (§3.12).
    

    Amp protects or mutes the moment signal arrivesShort in the cable or connector — unplug at the box end and test the cable → a damaged box → too many boxes on one channel (load too low).
    

    Amp shows over-temperatureBlocked ventilation (rack doors, cases, sun) → reduce level → tell the system owner. Don't keep restarting it.
    

    Amp won't power on, or keeps rebootingpowerCON locked? → mains present at the distro (ask an electrician — §12.15) → try one known-good amp on the same feed → swap the amp.
    

    Amp not showing in R1Ethernet cable and switch → laptop on the right network adapter and address range → duplicate Remote ID or IP → firewall on the laptop → for D6/D12, the CAN interface. D40/D90 Milan streams are a separate network from Dante (§8.2).
    

    Wrong box answers when you solo a channelPatch doesn't match the labels. Stop, trace each cable, fix the labels before anything else.
    

    System check flags a boxCable first (lock, swap) → then the box. A missing box, a dead driver or a damaged cable all look like an impedance change.
    

    Rattle or buzz at certain notes onlyUsually mechanical: loose grille, rigging hardware, a stand or something resting on the box. Not an amp fault.
    

    

    Watch it
    Don't change a setup, an output mode or an ArrayProcessing setting to "see if it helps" — on someone else's system that's not your call, and the wrong change can damage drivers. Gather the facts above and hand them over. Don't open amps or boxes; that's for the service department.
    

    Standard
    The fault finder in Support walks through these same checks as a conversation, and builds the "symptom, what changed, what I've checked, what I need" message for you at the end.
    

    


    6.20 d&b models — which box, which amp
    

    A field reference to the d&b amplifiers and loudspeakers you're likely to meet in UK hire stock and venues — current models, and the discontinued ones (d&b call them "heritage") that are still out working every week. Use it to work out what a box is, what drives it and what to watch for. The fault finder in Support reads these tables too, so you can ask it "what amp does a V8 need?" or "can a D20 run KSL?". Kit you've added to My equipment reference is marked My kit below.
    

    Standard
    The one rule that settles it on site: if the box's setup isn't in the amp's setup list (on its screen or in R1), that amp can't drive it. Firmware updates add setups over time, so an older amp that hasn't been updated may be missing a newer box. And with line arrays, the plan will say which setup each box gets.
    


    Reading the names
    

    

    8 / 12 in a line array
    The horizontal coverage: 8 = 80°, 12 = 120° (V8/V12, Y8/Y12, KSL8/KSL12, CCL8/CCL12, J8/J12). Same height and rigging, so the two can mix in one hang.
    

    P
    A point-source box from a line-array family (V7P, V10P, Y7P, Y10P).
    

    -SUB / -GSUB
    Subwoofer. GSUB is the ground-stack-only version; SUB versions can usually be flown with the array.
    

    -D
    A wider-dispersion version of the same box (E12-D, 10S-D, 12S-D, 24S-D).
    

    i (Yi8, KSLi12, ALi60…)
    The installation version: same sound, different cabinet finish and fixings. Venue kit, not hire stock.
    

    Arc / Line / AP / PS
    Setup variants for array boxes: Arc for boxes in the curved part of a hang, Line for the straight part, AP when the array runs ArrayProcessing, PS for a box used on its own as a point source. Take them from the plan, box by box.

    Q-SeriesQ1 (line array), Q7, Q10, Q-SUBDiscontinued compact system, still common: Q1 hangs as a small array, Q7/Q10 are point source.D6, D12, D20, D80. On newer amps, check the setup list.
    

    M-SeriesM2, M4, M6, MAX2 (older: MAX, MAX12)Stage monitors. M4 and M6 have both active and passive setups; MAX2 is the low-profile wedge.M4, M6, MAX2: most d&b amps. M2: D80 or D90 only — not D20 or D40.
    

    B-Series subsB4, B6, B8, B10, B10N, B12, B22-SUB (older: B1, B2)Subwoofers to go with the point-source ranges. Several can be set up cardioid.Most d&b amps — check the setup list for the larger ones.
    

    C-Series, CiC4, C6, C7 and the Ci install boxesOld discontinued ranges. Still found in venues and older stock.Check the amp's setup list; older installs often run D6/D12 or E-PAC.
    

    

    Watch it
    "Not D20" means exactly that: the setup isn't in the amp, and running the box on a linear or wrong setup leaves it unprotected. If the plan pairs a box with an amp this table says can't drive it, stop and ask before you rack it up — the plan, or the stock list, may be wrong.
    

    Also seen
    Alongside the amps you'll meet d&b's network and processing boxes: DS10 (Dante to AES bridge), DS20 (Dante to Milan), DS100 (the Soundscape processor), plus R90 touchscreen remotes in installs. And installation-only loudspeaker ranges — U-Series and the "i" versions above — that you'll see in venues rather than on the shelf.
    

    Go deeper
    Each product page on dbaudio.com has the manual and datasheet, and the amp firmware release notes carry the full list of setups each amp supports. When this table and a current d&b document disagree, the d&b document wins — and tell whoever looks after this pack.
    

    


    6.21 L-Acoustics — the same ideas, different names
    

    If you know d&b, you already understand L-Acoustics: amps with built-in processing, loudspeaker-specific settings, prediction software and a remote-control app. The names change.
    

    

    Jobd&bL-Acoustics
    


    Amps with processingD20, D40, D80, D90Amplified controllers: LA4X, LA12X, LA7.16, LA2Xi
    

    Speaker-specific settingsSetup (per channel)Preset — loaded from the amp's preset library
    

    Remote control & monitoringR1LA Network Manager
    

    PredictionArrayCalcSoundvision
